# Official Dual-Mom Marriage Quality Audit & Rating Template
## For Internal Couple Use Only — No PTA Judges, Nosy Grandmas, or Side-Eyeing Park Moms Allowed
Welcome, tired, snack-wielding queen! You and your wife/spouse/partner-in-toddler-chaos have already outperformed 99% of heterosexual dad couples just by remembering both kids’ birthdays and only crying in the Target parking lot once a month. This audit is not for bragging on Instagram, arguing about who does more, or proving to your conservative uncle that your marriage is “valid.” It’s for gently roasting each other, celebrating your unhinged little wins, and remembering that even when the house looks like a glitter bomb exploded and no one has brushed their hair in 4 days, you’re on the same team.
### Non-Negotiable Ground Rules (No Cheating):
1. You may not complete this audit within 24 hours of a kid-related stomach bug, a PTA meeting, or a fight about who left the milk out.
2. “I packed 22 snacks for the class party” does not count as a get-out-of-jail-free card for forgetting to pay the water bill.
3. Every audit comes with a mandatory 15-point bonus for every child that is currently alive, not currently covered in paint, and hasn’t called a stranger a “poopy head” in public in the last 72 hours.
4. If you get into a fight while filling this out, you both automatically get a perfect score and have to go get tacos immediately. No takebacks.
---
### Audit Metadata
- Participant 1 Nickname: (e.g. The One Who Forgets Lunchboxes, The One Who Still Hasn’t Hung The Gallery Wall 5 Years In)
- Participant 2 Nickname: (e.g. The One Who Hides Chocolate From The Kids, The One Who Accidentally Signed Us Up For 3 Soccer Leagues)
- Number Of Human Kids: ____
- Number Of Fur Kids That You Treat Like Human Kids: ____
- Number Of Half-Cold Coffee Mugs Currently On Your Counter: ____ (add 2 bonus points per mug)
---
*Co-Parenting Tag Team Synchronization Score (1-10 Scale)*
This metric measures how well you function as a chaotic, Goldfish-wielding unit when shit hits the fan. No bonus points for looking perfect on Instagram—we’re grading real life here.
#### Scoring Rubric:
- +1 point if you can communicate an entire sentence (e.g. “The kid just peed their pants, get a change of clothes”) via eye contact across a crowded birthday party.
- +2 points if you never, ever dump a “the kid just drew on the couch with permanent marker” problem on the other person the second they walk in the door from work.
- -3 points if you have ever faked snoring to avoid getting up with a barfing toddler at 2am.
- -5 points if you have ever used “I had a harder day” as an excuse to dodge bedtime duty for 3 nights in a row.
- +5 bonus points if you both remembered class snack day and showed up with extra cheddar Goldfish (the holy grail of parent wins).
#### Score Key:
1/10 = You both pretended to be asleep until the kid climbed in between you and peed the bed.
10/10 = You took turns holding the barfing kid’s hair back, brought each other Gatorade and a granola bar mid-vomit-session, and then laughed about how the kid threw up on the only nice couch you own.
---
### Extended Family Drama Navigation Score (1-10 Scale)
Measures how well you team up to handle the endless parade of nosy questions from people who still think you “need a man around the house.”
#### Scoring Rubric:
- +1 point if you both make the exact same deadpan joke about “the patriarchy being unnecessary” when your grandma asks when you’ll get a “real dad” for the kids.
- +3 points if you tag-team to shut down the uncle who tries to debate your marriage validity at Thanksgiving.
- -4 points if one of you agreed to let the in-laws stay for 10 days without consulting the other.
- -2 points if one of you caves and lets the grandma give the kids 17 lollipops even though you agreed no sugar after 5pm.
---
*Division Of Unseen Mom Labor Fairness Score (1-10 Scale)*
Ah, the secret stuff no one posts about: the mental load of remembering pediatrician phone numbers, soccer cleat sizes, allergy lists, birthday party RSVP deadlines, and that the youngest will only eat crusts cut off their sandwiches in the shape of dinosaurs. There is no “default mom” in this household—we’re grading how evenly you split that chaos.
#### Scoring Rubric:
- +1 point if both of you have the pediatrician’s phone number saved in your phones (no, “I just text you” doesn’t count).
- +2 points if you rotate the “default parent” duty every month so neither of you is always the one getting the 10am call from the school nurse.
- -3 points if either of you has ever said “I didn’t know we needed more milk” when the carton was empty for 36 hours and you both drink 2 glasses a day. No, “you never told me” is not a valid defense.
- -5 points if one of you dumped the entire Halloween costume planning process on the other person 2 days before October 31.
- +4 bonus points if you have a shared reminder list that both of you actually check (no passive aggressive sticky notes on the fridge allowed).
#### Score Key:
1/10 = One of you has a running Google Doc of 497 household deadlines and the other doesn’t know the kid’s 2nd grade teacher’s first name.
10/10 = You split all the invisible work so evenly that neither of you has had a “why am I the only one who does everything” breakdown in over 3 months.
---
### Public Parenting Flex Score (1-10 Scale)
Measures how cool you two look as a unit to every other overstressed mom at the park.
#### Scoring Rubric:
- +1 point if you show up to every school event in matching (intentional or not) mom jeans and iced coffee.
- +3 points if you teamed up to get the teacher to stop assigning 2 hours of homework to a 7-year-old.
- -4 points if either of you agreed to chaperone the middle school dance without consulting the other.
- +5 points if you ditched a PTA meeting halfway through to go get tacos together.
---
*Post-Kid-Beddate Intimacy & Leisure Alignment Score (1-10 Scale)*
Let’s be real: for dual-mom households, “intimacy” is 70% folding tiny socks side by side while roasting the PTA group chat, 20% making out on the couch while half-watching a Netflix show, and 10% fancy date nights that require 3 hours of childcare planning and actually showering. We’re grading all of it.
#### Scoring Rubric:
- +1 point if you both agree that no kid-related problems (permission slips, lice outbreaks, missing stuffed animals) are allowed to be discussed after 8:30pm.
- +2 points if you prioritize low-effort couch time in your rattiest sweatpants over expensive “date nights” that require you to wear real pants and pay $60 for a babysitter.
- -3 points if you fall asleep mid-episode of your shared show 3 nights in a row.
- -5 points if you bring up a school-related problem 2 minutes into a makeout session.
- +4 bonus points if you can successfully sneak a 20-minute snuggle session in before one of you remembers you left the crockpot on.
#### Score Key:
1/10 = The only thing you say to each other after bedtime is “did you lock the front door?” before passing out.
10/10 = You alternate between making out and folding 19 pairs of tiny underwear while roasting the mom who tried to ban cupcakes from class parties.
---
### Wildcard Bonus Points (Add All Applicable)
+3 points: You both wore the same “World’s Best Mom” shirt on Mother’s Day without planning it
+5 points: You successfully convinced your kids that broccoli is candy for 3 whole days
+7 points: You haven’t had a fight about screen time limits in 2 weeks
-10 points: One of you bought a puppy without asking the other
+15 points: The puppy is really cute and you both love it now
---
### Final Score & Official Marriage Rating
Add up all your points, plus the mandatory kid-survival bonus points, then find your tier below:
#### 90-100 Points: ELITE DUAL-MOM MARRIAGE
Congratulations! You two are the couple every other mom at the park stares at jealously. You have your chaotic moments, but you’re a perfectly synced team. **Reward:** Hire a babysitter, order 2 bottles of fancy wine, and make a rule that no one mentions the kids for 2 whole hours. If you can make it 20 minutes, that’s still a win.
#### 70-89 Points: SOLID, FUNCTIONAL DUAL-MOM MARRIAGE
You have your off days, but who doesn’t? You’re both trying your best, and that’s more than enough. **Reward:** Split a pint of your favorite ice cream after bedtime tonight. No folding laundry allowed while you eat it.
#### 50-69 Points: ROUGH PATCH, BUT YOU GOT THIS
Chances are one of the kids had strep throat 3 times this month, the car broke down, and the dryer ate 12 socks. You’re both tired, and that’s okay. **Reward:** Take turns taking a solo 2-hour nap this weekend. No questions asked, no chore guilt allowed.
#### Below 50 Points: EMERGENCY RELATIONSHIP RESET
First, order takeout. Second, hand each other a glass of wine. Third, remember that time you both laughed so hard you cried when the kid called the principal a poopy head? That’s worth 50 extra points. Bump your score up to the 70-89 tier and take the ice cream reward. You’ve earned it.
---
*Audit completed on: ____  Signed, ____ & ____ (the best mom team your kids ever had)*

1/10 = The only thing you say to each other after bedtime is “did you lock the front door?” before passing out.

+3 points: You both wore the same “World’s Best Mom” shirt on Mother’s Day without planning it
+5 points: You successfully convinced your kids that broccoli is candy for 3 whole days
+7 points: You haven’t had a fight about screen time limits in 2 weeks
-10 points: One of you bought a puppy without asking the other

# Lecture Outline: La La Land: Dreamers, Nostalgia, and the Bittersweet Magic of "What If"
Target Audience: Adaptable for high school English/media classes or undergraduate film/cultural studies students | Estimated Runtime: 90 minutes (adjustable for shorter class periods)

---

## Section 1: Opening Hook & Context Setting (15 mins)
### Content & Activities:
1. Icebreaker: Play the 1-minute opening of the "Another Day of Sun" freeway number (no intro first to grab attention)
2. Interactive Poll (show of hands):
   - Raise your hand if you’ve seen La La Land before
   - Raise your hand if you left the movie angry or sad about the ending
   - Raise your hand if you’ve ever chased a creative, academic, or professional dream that felt impossible to pull off
3. Context Check (casual, pop-culture anchored):
   - Quick rundown of 2016 release: Damien Chazelle’s 10-year quest to make an original low-budget musical, his prior hit *Whiplash*
   - Reference the infamous 2017 Best Picture Oscar mix-up with *Moonlight* as a light cultural touchpoint
   - Frame the film’s 2010s cultural resonance: post-2008 recession-era young people navigating gig work, constant rejection, and pressure to "follow your dream"
### Key Takeaway for Students:
La La Land is both a nostalgic throwback to old Hollywood and a very modern story about the trade-offs of growing up that hit a nerve for audiences its age.

---

## Section 2: Deconstructing the Musical: Love Letter and Subversion (25 mins)
### Content & Activities:
1. Part A: The Old Hollywood Homage
   - Mini clip comparison: 30-second clip of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers’ *Swing Time* dance number + 30-second clip of Mia and Sebastian’s planetarium dance
   - Discussion Prompt: What visual or tonal parallels do you notice? Why would Chazelle reference 1940s/50s musicals for a 2016 story?
   - Formal technique deep dive (easy to spot for casual viewers):
     - Cinemascope wide aspect ratio (used for classic musicals to make dance numbers feel grand)
     - Stitched "one-take" shots that mimic the unbroken energy of live stage musicals
     - Color coding: Mia’s signature bright yellow, Sebastian’s signature deep blue; blended tones when their dreams align, muted grays/browns when they drift apart
2. Part B: The Subversion of Musical Tropes
   - Lecture bite: Classic musicals frame love and success as perfectly compatible rewards for dreaming big. La La Land wraps its fantasy around very un-musical-like realism.
   - Interactive Check-In: What’s one moment in the movie that felt too messy or sad to be in a classic musical? (e.g., their dinner fight, Mia’s failed one-woman show, no grand last-minute run to the airport)
### Key Takeaway for Students:
Chazelle uses nostalgia for old musicals to make his hard, modern message about sacrifice feel familiar and safe to process.

---

## Section 3: Core Conflict: Dreams vs. Connection (25 mins)
### Content & Activities:
1. Think-Pair-Share (5 mins): Turn to a partner and answer: If you had to choose between a once-in-a-lifetime career opportunity that required moving across the world and a serious, happy relationship, what would you pick? Why? (No "right answer" framing!)
2. Character Arc Breakdown + Critical Nuance:
   - Break down Sebastian’s arc: His obsession with "saving jazz" as a marker of identity, the tension between artistic integrity and commercial stability (his time in the pop-jazz band)
   - Break down Mia’s arc: Her journey from barista to actress, the vulnerability of putting your creative self out for repeated rejection
   - Introduce common critical debates to avoid one-note praise of the film:
     1. The "white savior of jazz" critique: Sebastian, a white man, is framed as the sole protector of a Black art form, while Black jazz artists are sidelined as supporting characters or foils (e.g., John Legend’s character Keith, framed as "selling out" jazz)
     2. The underdevelopment of Mia’s interior life: We get far more context for Sebastian’s passion for jazz than we do for Mia’s love of acting
   - Full Class Discussion: Do these critiques change how you view the movie? Why or why not?
### Key Takeaway for Students:
La La Land’s central tension isn’t about "choosing the right thing"—it’s about the quiet reality that some of our most important desires can’t coexist, no matter how much we want them to.

---

## Section 4: The Ending That Defined the Film: The "What If" Montage (20 mins)
### Content & Activities:
1. Clip: Play the full 7-minute ending montage (from Mia spotting Seb’s club sign to the final shared smile)
2. Formal Breakdown: Point out how Chazelle signals the shift to fantasy without dialogue: softer lighting, faster editing, musical callbacks to every major number in the film, muted pastels instead of the bold primary colors used for real-life scenes
3. Full Class Discussion:
   1. Why do you think so many people find this ending satisfying even though Mia and Sebastian don’t end up together?
   2. What does their final smile mean to you? Is it regret? Gratitude? Both?
   3. How does this ending speak to how we all romanticize our own "what ifs"—the paths we didn’t take in life?
### Key Takeaway for Students:
La La Land doesn’t mourn the love or dreams that didn’t work out—it celebrates the ways those people and goals shaped us into who we are.

---

## Closing & Extensions (5 mins)
1. Closing Line: "La La Land is called a fantasy, but its most honest message is that no life is perfect, no choice is without loss, and that’s okay. The dreams and people we love don’t have to last forever to matter."
2. Optional Exit Ticket: Write down one "what if" in your own life that this movie made you think about, and one small takeaway you’re leaving with today.
3. Optional Homework Extensions:
   - Watch Chazelle’s *Whiplash* and write a 1-page reflection on how both films explore the cost of ambition
   - Read one published critique of La La Land’s treatment of jazz and write a 1-page response agreeing or disagreeing with the author’s argument

# The Banana Peel Is Way More Than A Slapstick Prop—it’s A Biological Overachiever

Last month, I spent $12 on a box of perfectly ripe Cavendish bananas, all to film a TikTok where I’d slip on a peel, land gracefully on a couch cushion, and go viral. Instead, I slipped, landed directly on my tailbone, and watched my roommate laugh so hard they spilled their iced coffee all over my laptop. I was disappointed that the stunt didn’t work, and even more disappointed that I wasted a dozen perfectly good bananas just to look like a fool in front of my cat. What I didn’t know while I was icing my bruised butt that night is that the banana peel wasn’t just a slapstick prop—it was a highly evolved, underappreciated biological miracle with more specialized parts than a luxury apartment building.

Let’s peel back the layers (sorry, I had to) and meet the tiny, hardworking parts that make banana peels the unsung heroes of the produce aisle.

## *Peel Epidermis*
The outermost layer of every banana peel is the *Peel Epidermis*, a waxy, waterproof suit of armor that evolved to protect the soft, squishy fruit inside from tropical rain, harsh sun, and nosy insects. This thin, shiny layer is made of cutin, a fatty polymer that repels water so well it makes rain jackets look amateur. If you’ve ever left a banana on your counter for three days and it didn’t turn into a soggy mess like that sad bag of spinach you forgot in the back of your fridge, you have the *Peel Epidermis* to thank. It’s so tough and water-resistant that scientists have even experimented with using ground banana peel epidermis as a cheap, biodegradable alternative to plastic packaging. The only downside? It can’t protect against that one friend who squeezes every banana in the grocery store before picking one. No armor is perfect.

## *Stomatal Sentinels*
If you zoom in on a banana peel with a microscope (which I did, while recovering from my tailbone injury and waiting for my laptop to dry), you’ll see thousands of tiny, mouth-shaped pores called *Stomatal Sentinels*. These little guys are the peel’s security team, opening and closing on a strict schedule to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out while blocking fungi, pests, and the judgmental stares of your cat who still hasn’t forgiven you for the frisbee incident (we’ll get to that). When the banana is still growing on its tree, the stomata work in sync to keep the fruit healthy as it dangles in the tropical wind. Once you pick the banana, though, they panic. Away from their tree home, the stomata close up partially, which speeds up ripening and explains why bananas go from “perfectly yellow” to “brown mush” in the 12 hours you leave them in your work bag.

## *Lignin Underlayer*
Beneath the shiny epidermis sits the *Lignin Underlayer*, the peel’s resident bodybuilder. This thick, fibrous middle layer is made of lignin, the same tough polymer that makes tree bark hard enough to carve your initials into. Its whole job is to keep the delicate banana fruit safe from birds, squirrels, and overzealous grocery store squeezers. When a banana is unripe and green, this layer is so stiff you can use a green banana peel as a tiny frisbee (don’t try it, I did, and hit my cat. She’s still holding a grudge.) Scientists are even using unripe banana peel lignin to make cheap, sustainable vegan leather that smells faintly of fruit instead of a feedlot. As the banana ripens, though, the lignin breaks down, turning the peel floppy and easy to tear. It’s not being lazy—it’s just retiring after a long career of banana protection.

## *Slime Mucilage Glands*
We all know the banana peel’s most iconic superpower: its ability to make grown adults flail like a toddler in a ball pit before face-planting into a pile of groceries. What you might not know is that this isn’t an accident—it’s a deliberate defense mechanism courtesy of the *Slime Mucilage Glands* lining the peel’s soft inner surface. These tiny glands secrete a goopy mix of polysaccharides and water that’s so slippery, it won a team of Japanese scientists the 2014 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics for proving banana peels have a lower coefficient of friction than wet ice. Yes, cartoon logic is peer-reviewed science. Why would a peel evolve to be this slippery? In the wild, when an animal eats a banana and drops the peel on the forest floor, the slime makes it hard for pests or competing plants to root around near the peel’s leftover seeds, giving any potential new banana trees a chance to grow. For humans, it’s just an excuse to face-plant in front of your barista. Thanks, evolution.

## *Ethylene Ripening Switch*
If you’ve ever shoved a green banana in a paper bag with an apple to ripen it fast, you have the *Ethylene Ripening Switch* to thank for that hack. Every banana peel has specialized cells that produce ethylene, a gaseous hormone that acts like a remote control for the entire fruit’s ripening process. When the banana is still on the tree, the switch is flipped almost all the way off, keeping the fruit green and tough enough to survive wind and rain. Once picked, the switch flips on, flooding the peel and fruit with ethylene: it breaks down the lignin underlayer, turns the fruit’s starchy flesh into sweet, sugary goodness, and changes the peel’s color from green to yellow to that unappetizing brown. Grocery stores use this switch to their advantage, shipping bananas green and gassing them with low levels of ethylene in warehouses so they all turn bright yellow at the exact same time, like a synchronized swim team for fruit. I was disappointed last week when my entire banana bunch turned brown overnight after I left them next to a bag of avocados (also big ethylene producers), and honestly, the peels were too—they followed the ripening script perfectly, and I missed the window.

## *Post-Peel Microbial Zoo*
You might think once you toss a banana peel in the compost or trash, its job is done. But the *Post-Peel Microbial Zoo* is just getting started. A single used banana peel is home to more than 100 species of bacteria, fungi, and tiny nematodes, all ready to chow down on the peel’s leftover nutrients and turn it into rich, fertile soil for new plants. This is why banana peels are the MVPs of home compost piles: they break down in as little as two weeks, feed all the good microbes in your pile, and add so much potassium that your tomato plants will grow like they’re on steroids. It’s also why people swear by rubbing banana peels on their houseplant leaves, their acne, or their teeth to whiten them. Full disclosure: the teeth whitening and acne hacks don’t work, and I can confirm that rubbing a banana peel on your face will just make you smell like a tropical smoothie and attract a horde of fruit flies. But the plant trick? Chef’s kiss. Just don’t toss a peel on the sidewalk, unless you want to be responsible for some poor schmuck’s failed TikTok stunt. Trust me, that schmuck will be very disappointed.

So next time you toss a banana peel in the compost, give it a little nod. It spent weeks protecting your snack, mastered the science of ripening, and evolved a superpower so iconic it’s been in cartoons for 100 years. It’s not garbage—it’s a tiny, yellow biological legend. Just don’t step on it.

As the banana ripens, though, the lignin breaks down, turning the peel floppy and easy to tear. It’s not being lazy—it’s just retiring after a long career of banana protection.

## *Slime Mucilage Glands*
We all know the banana peel’s most iconic superpower: its ability to make grown adults flail like a toddler in a ball pit before face-planting into a pile of groceries. What you might not know is that this isn’t an accident—it’s a deliberate defense mechanism courtesy of the *Slime Mucilage Glands* lining the peel’s soft inner surface. These tiny glands secrete a goopy mix of polysaccharides and water that’s so slippery, it won a team of Japanese scientists the 2014 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics for proving banana peels have a lower coefficient of friction than wet ice. Yes, cartoon logic is peer-reviewed science. Why would a peel evolve to be this slippery? In the wild, when an animal eats a banana and drops the peel on the forest floor, the slime makes it hard for pests or competing plants to root around near the peel’s leftover seeds, giving any potential new banana trees a chance to grow. For humans, it’s just an excuse to face-plant in front of your barista. Thanks, evolution.

## *Ethylene Ripening Switch*
If you’ve ever shoved a green banana in a paper bag with an apple to ripen it fast, you have the *Ethylene Ripening Switch* to thank for that hack. Every banana peel has specialized cells that produce ethylene, a gaseous hormone that acts like a remote control for the entire fruit’s ripening process. When the banana is still on the tree, the switch is flipped almost all the way off, keeping the fruit green and tough enough to survive wind and rain. Once picked, the switch flips on, flooding the peel and fruit with ethylene: it breaks down the lignin underlayer, turns the fruit’s starchy flesh into sweet, sugary goodness, and changes the peel’s color from green to yellow to that unappetizing brown. Grocery stores use this switch to their advantage, shipping bananas green and gassing them with low levels of ethylene in warehouses so they all turn bright yellow at the exact same time, like a synchronized swim team for fruit. I was disappointed last week when my entire banana bunch turned brown overnight after I left them next to a bag of avocados (also big ethylene producers), and honestly, the peels were too—they followed the ripening script perfectly, and I missed the window.

## *Post-Peel Microbial Zoo*
You might think once you toss a banana peel in the compost or trash, its job is done. But the *Post-Peel Microbial Zoo* is just getting started. A single used banana peel is home to more than 100 species of bacteria, fungi, and tiny nematodes, all ready to chow down on the peel’s leftover nutrients and turn it into rich, fertile soil for new plants. This is why banana peels are the MVPs of home compost piles: they break down in as little as two weeks, feed all the good microbes in your pile, and add so much potassium that your tomato plants will grow like they’re on steroids. It’s also why people swear by rubbing banana peels on their houseplant leaves, their acne, or their teeth to whiten them. Full disclosure: the teeth whitening and acne hacks don’t work, and I can confirm that rubbing a banana peel on your face will just make you smell like a tropical smoothie and attract a horde of fruit flies. But the plant trick? Chef’s kiss. Just don’t toss a peel on the sidewalk, unless you want to be responsible for some poor schmuck’s failed TikTok stunt. Trust me, that schmuck will be very disappointed.

So next time you toss a banana peel in the compost, give it a little nod. It spent weeks protecting your snack, mastered the science of ripening, and evolved a superpower so iconic it’s been in cartoons for 100 years. It’s not garbage—it’s a tiny, yellow biological legend. Just don’t step on it.

"# How to Raise Cause Awareness That Sticks (And Doesn’t Disappear After 48 Hours)
Last year, I volunteered with a local grassroots group working to expand free after-school programming for middle schoolers in our low-income neighborhood. Our first campaign attempt flopped hard: we spent weeks designing a glossy infographic citing national stats about after-school care gaps, paid $300 to boost it on Instagram, and ended up with 1,400 likes, 62 shares, and only 17 sign-ups for our volunteer orientation. We’d gotten eyes on our cause, but no one felt connected enough to act. Over the next seven months, we completely reworked our strategy, and by the end of the school year, we’d raised enough funding to launch three new after-school sites, with 120 active volunteers and 210 enrolled students. Below are the five core strategies that turned our fleeting social media attention into meaningful, action-driving awareness.
Section 1: Lead With Hyper-Specific, Consented Human Narratives (Not Just Statistics)
Stats are critical for proving the scope of a problem, but they rarely motivate people to care on their own. Our initial campaign lead with “1 in 3 local middle schoolers have no supervised care after school” — a true, important number, but one that felt abstract to most people scrolling their feeds. We shifted gears after we connected with Lila, a 13-year-old in our neighborhood who’d been walking home alone for two years after school, often skipping meals because her mom worked late and couldn’t leave food out for her. With Lila and her mom’s full consent, we shared a 90-second Reel of Lila talking about hiding snacks in her backpack and wishing there was a place she could hang out with friends and do homework after school. That reel got half the likes of our original infographic, but it drove 12x more volunteer sign-ups and 18x more small donations. The key here is consent and agency: never share someone’s story without their explicit approval, and let them lead how their story is framed, rather than crafting a “sad narrative” for clicks.
Section 2: Meet Your Audience Where They Already Gather (Don’t Expect Them to Seek You Out)
Our first mistake was assuming our target audience was on Instagram. The people most invested in local after-school care weren’t 20-something content creators — they were working parents, neighborhood retirees, local small business owners, and middle school teachers, most of whom spent time on Nextdoor, local parent Facebook Groups, and in-person at the public library and elementary school pick-up lines. We printed flyers with Lila’s photo (again, with permission) and posted them at the library, the local grocery store, and all three neighborhood elementary schools. We joined 11 local parent and neighborhood groups, and shared Lila’s story as a personal update rather than a formal solicitation. We also partnered with three local PTA leaders and a popular neighborhood babysitter with 900 followers on Facebook, who shared our campaign to their own networks. Over 75% of our volunteer sign-ups and donations came from these in-person and hyper-local online spaces, not our public Instagram page. For local causes especially, a trusted share from a community member with 800 followers is far more valuable than a shoutout from a celebrity with 2 million.
Section 3: Tie Every Awareness Touchpoint to a Low-Stakes, Immediate Action
One of the biggest pitfalls of cause awareness campaigns is asking people to “spread the word” with no clear next step. Shouting “raise awareness!” leaves people confused and unlikely to engage further, because they don’t know what that actually means. For every piece of content we created, every flyer we printed, and every in-person conversation we had, we offered three tiny, no-obligation actions people could take in 60 seconds or less: 1) Send a pre-written email to the school board asking them to allocate funding for after-school care, 2) Sign up for a 1-hour volunteer shift to help pack snack bags for students, or 3) Drop a box of granola bars or art supplies at the library drop-off bin. No one had to donate $100, no one had to commit to volunteering every week, and we celebrated every small action equally instead of shaming people for not doing more. We found that 68% of people who interacted with our campaign took at least one of these actions, because the barrier to entry was so low.
Section 4: Build Recurring, Community-Led Touchpoints to Keep Awareness Top of Mind
Awareness isn’t a one-and-done campaign. Even the most viral post will fade from people’s memories within 48 hours if there’s nothing to reinforce it. To keep our cause top of mind, we launched monthly “Neighbor Coffee Hours” at the local library, where anyone could stop by for 20 minutes or two hours, grab a free coffee, chat with other community members, and hear updates from the after-school program students and staff. We didn’t ask people to work or donate — we just wanted to build connection around the cause. We also hosted a quarterly “Student Story Slam,” where after-school program students could share art, poems, or short stories about their experiences, with the events open to the entire community. We shared recordings of these slams on our social media and submitted write-ups to the local newspaper, so the cause stayed in front of people even when we weren’t actively fundraising or recruiting volunteers. By the time the school board voted on our funding request, over 300 community members showed up to the meeting in support, because they’d built personal connections to the cause over months, not just seen one post online.
Section 5: Measure Meaningful Impact, Not Just Vanity Metrics
It’s easy to get caught up in likes, shares, and follower count, but those metrics don’t tell you if you’ve actually changed anyone’s perspective or motivated them to act. Instead of tracking social media vanity metrics, we focused on three core categories of impact: 1) Action metrics: number of volunteer sign-ups, donations, emails sent to the school board, and supply drop-offs, 2) Perspective metrics: short, anonymous surveys of people who interacted with our campaign asking if they learned something new about after-school care gaps in our neighborhood, and 3) Long-term behavior metrics: follow-up surveys three and six months after launch asking if people had taken any ongoing action to support the cause, from volunteering regularly to voting for school board candidates who prioritized after-school care. By the end of our campaign, 91% of survey respondents said they’d learned something new about local care gaps, and 72% said they’d taken at least one ongoing action to support the program. Those numbers told us we’d built meaningful, lasting awareness, not just a fleeting viral moment.
At the end of the day, cause awareness isn’t about going viral or looking good on social media. It’s about helping people see themselves in the cause, and giving them the tools to show up in ways that feel doable. When you center the voices of the people most affected, meet your audience where they are, give them clear small actions, build ongoing community, and track what actually matters, you’ll build awareness that sticks long after the social media algorithm moves on to the next trend. What’s a strategy that’s worked for your cause? Drop it in the comments below!"

# The Princess of Honey and the Dragon of Stories
Once upon a time, in the sun-dappled Kingdom of Bramblehold, where apple orchards stretched as far as the eye could see and spiced honey mead flowed at every village feast, there lived a princess named Liora. Unlike the princesses in nursery tales, Liora cared little for silk gowns or suitors’ flowery poems; her favorite place was the royal apiary, where she tended hives side by side with village beekeepers, her calloused hands dotted with old stings and a thin pale scar snaking across her left cheek—earned at twelve, falling from an apple bough while rescuing a lost swarm.

When Liora was nineteen, a terrible blight swept through Bramblehold’s hives. The bees grew listless, stopped making honey, and died by the thousands. Apple blossoms withered unpollinated, the mead cellars ran dry, and the kingdom faced famine before the year’s end. The old wise women of the hills proclaimed the only cure was to breed Bramblehold’s remaining weak bees with the hardy wild hives that thrived on the Crag of Whispering Echoes—a jagged mountain peak that had been home to Vorath the Amber-Scaled, a fearsome dragon, for over two hundred years.

No one had spoken to Vorath in living memory. All tales said he hoarded mountains of gold and ate any maidens foolish enough to climb his crag. King Theron, Liora’s father, proclaimed a great reward: any knight who slayed the dragon and brought back the wild hives would win Liora’s hand in marriage and half the kingdom.

Liora was furious. She knew killing the dragon would only send the wild bees fleeing, for no creature knew the crag’s clover slopes and hidden hollows better than the beast who had lived there for centuries. So at dawn the next day, she snuck out of the castle with a jar of the last good mead she’d brewed, her leather-bound notebook of bee sketches, and her tattered linen bee veil, and began the climb up the Crag of Whispering Echoes.

She was halfway to the peak when a shadow fell over her, and a deep, rumbling voice shook the rocks at her feet. “Trespasser,” Vorath rumbled, his amber scales glinting like solidified honey in the sun, smoke curling from his nostrils. “The knights who climb this crag come with lances and lies of glory. What do you bring, soft thing with bee-sting pricks on your knuckles?”

Liora did not flinch. She held up the earthen jar of mead, its cork sealed with beeswax stamped with her personal bee crest. “I bring an apology, and a trade. My kingdom’s hives are dying. The only clover sweet enough to sustain them grows on your slopes, and your wild bees are the only ones strong enough to breed with ours. I ask for three hives, and permission to send my beekeepers to harvest clover here, in return for a jar of mead every full moon, and whatever else you might name that I can give.”

Vorath snorted, a tiny puff of flame melting a patch of moss at her boots. “And what makes you think I would trade the bounty of my mountain for swill from a king’s larder?”

Liora replied, her chin tilted so her scar caught the sun: “It’s not the king’s larder. It’s mine. I brewed it myself, with honey from my own apiary hives, the ones I’ve tended since I was seven. It’s not swill. It’s the last good jar of mead left in Bramblehold.”

Curious, Vorath bent his great head and sniffed the jar. The scent of clover and cinnamon wrapped around him, sweeter than any gold he had ever smelled. He had not spoken to anyone who did not want to kill him in over a hundred years. “Come,” he rumbled, turning toward the mouth of his cave. “See what I hoard, and then we will bargain.”

Liora followed, her heart thudding but unafraid. When she stepped into the cave, she gasped. There were no piles of gold, no heaps of stolen jewels. Instead, shelves carved into the rock stretched from floor to ceiling, stacked with stone tablets, rolled scrolls, carved wooden figurines, and tattered tapestries. “I do not hoard gold,” Vorath said, settling onto a bed of moss at the cave’s center. “Gold rusts, melts, is stolen. I hoard stories. The knights who come? They all have the same boring story: I want glory, I want gold, I want a princess’s hand. No heart. No texture.”

Liora wandered the shelves, her fingers brushing a stone tablet carved with the image of a woman in a bee veil, surrounded by swarms of bees. “That’s my grandmother,” she breathed. “I thought all stories of her were lost when the old abbey burned down when I was a baby.”

“It was told to me by a traveling monk 120 years ago,” Vorath rumbled. “One of my favorites. She could sing to bees, and they would do whatever she asked.”

Liora replied, her voice soft with wonder as she traced the carving: “I would trade you a hundred new stories for those hives. Stories of my bees, of the village children who sneak into my orchard to steal tart green apples, of old Mara the baker who sings sea shanties while she kneads bread, even the silly story of how my father once tried to milk a goat and got kicked in the trousers. I can write them down for you, every full moon when I bring the mead.”

Vorath’s great tail twitched, the tip tapping a happy rhythm against the rock. No one had ever offered him stories before. Before he could respond, the sound of clanking armor and shouting echoed up the crag. A band of knights, sent by the king to rescue Liora and slay the dragon, burst into the cave, lances raised. “Surrender the princess, beast!” the lead knight yelled. “Or we will run you through!”

Vorath tensed, smoke billowing from his jaws, but Liora stepped quickly between him and the knights, her bee veil fluttering around her ankles. “Put down your lances,” she said sharply. “He is not our enemy.”

The lead knight sputtered. “Princess, he has bewitched you! The king will pay a king’s ransom for your return, and we will slay the beast and bring back the hives!”

“Gold will not save our hives,” Liora replied, sharp as a bee’s stinger. “A story outlasts kings. It outlasts gold. It feeds the soul in a way no coin ever could. Now go, and tell my father the dragon is our ally, not our foe. And if he sends more knights with lances, he will have no hives, no honey, and no daughter to marry off for a quick fix.”

The knights, stunned by her fury, stumbled back down the crag. When they told the king what had happened, he was furious at first—but when Liora returned that evening with a jar of wild honey and a promise that the hives would recover, he relented.

The trade was struck. Every full moon, Liora climbed the crag with a jar of mead and a scroll of new stories for Vorath. He taught her the old bee lore he had collected over centuries: songs to calm swarms and tricks to help hives survive harsh winters. Bramblehold’s hives recovered, sweeter and more bountiful than ever, and the kingdom’s mead became famous across the realm.

When Liora became queen a few years later, she declared the Crag of Whispering Echoes a sacred site, and built a small stone cottage at its foot for travelers who came to share their stories with Vorath. Knights no longer came to slay the dragon; they came to listen to his tales, and to leave stories of their own.

And for the rest of their days, neither queen nor dragon ever wanted for mead, or stories, or a friend who saw them for who they truly were—not what the world assumed they ought to be.

Often reduced to a caricature of kite-flying whimsy or the face of the hundred-dollar bill, Benjamin Franklin was the quintessential American Enlightenment figure: a self-made printer, scientist, diplomat, and founding father whose life of relentless curiosity, civic devotion, and moral evolution mirrored the messy, aspirational identity of the nation he helped build.
Born in Boston in 1706 as the 15th of 17 children to Josiah Franklin, a poor candle and soap maker, Franklin’s formal education ended at age 10, when he was pulled out of school to work in his father’s shop. At 12, he was apprenticed to his older brother James, a printer, where he honed a love of words and a talent for subversive wit. At 16, he began writing anonymous letters to his brother’s newspaper under the pseudonym Silence Dogood, a sharp-tongued middle-aged widow who mocked Puritan hypocrisy and advocated for women’s education. When James discovered the ruse and punished Franklin for the prank, the 17-year-old ran away, first to New York, then to Philadelphia, arriving with only a dollar in his pocket and three loaves of bread tucked under his arms—one to eat, two to give to a poor mother and child he had met on the voyage. That arrival, equal parts scrappy and generous, would come to define his life: a man who pulled himself up by his bootstraps, but never forgot to lift others along the way.
Within a decade of his arrival, Franklin had built a printing empire, buying the struggling Pennsylvania Gazette and turning it into the most widely read newspaper in the colonies. In 1733, he launched Poor Richard’s Almanack, a yearly collection of weather forecasts, farming tips, and aphorisms that would sell 10,000 copies a year for 25 years, making Franklin a household name. Lines like “A penny saved is a penny earned” and “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise” were not just empty platitudes; they were the blueprint for a distinctly American ethos of practical industry and self-improvement. But Franklin’s ambition extended far beyond personal wealth. Convinced that a thriving democracy depended on an educated public, he founded the Library Company of Philadelphia in 1731, the first public lending library in the colonies, followed by the Union Fire Company (the colonies’ first volunteer fire department), the Pennsylvania Hospital, the Academy of Philadelphia (which later became the University of Pennsylvania), and a standardized colonial postal system. Each of these projects was rooted in Franklin’s core belief that ordinary people, working together, could build a better community than any monarch or aristocrat could design for them.
Franklin’s curiosity extended beyond civic life to the natural world, where he turned a casual hobby into groundbreaking scientific discovery. After attending a lecture on electricity in Boston in 1743, he began experimenting with static charges in his spare time, eventually developing a theory that lightning was a form of electricity, not a supernatural act of divine wrath. In 1752, he tested his theory with the now-famous kite experiment, flying a silk kite strung with wire into a thunderstorm and capturing a charge in a Leyden jar via a key tied to the kite’s string. He went on to invent the lightning rod, which saved thousands of buildings from fire, as well as bifocal glasses, the energy-efficient Franklin stove, and a flexible urinary catheter designed to ease his brother’s kidney stone pain. Crucially, he refused to patent any of his inventions, writing, “As we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours; and this we should do freely and generously.”

But his loyalty to the crown shattered in 1773, when he was publicly humiliated before the Privy Council for leaking letters written by Massachusetts governor Thomas Hutchinson that called for the suppression of colonial liberties. Fifteenth of seventeen, born to tallow and flame,
Boston, 1706—no fortune to claim.
Two years of school, then a printer’s bent hand,
wrote Silence Dogood’s wit, sly and unplanned.
Ran at seventeen, bread loaves under each arm,
to Philly, where a new world could charm.

He bought the Gazette, then the almanac’s page,
Poor Richard’s wit turned every cottage’s sage.
A penny saved, a friend kept true,
wisdom stitched into the work he drew.
Built the first library, fire corps, hospital hall,
wove community from thin colonial wall.

Curiosity hummed in his spare, busy hours,
chased sparks that tore through the summer sky’s powers.
Kite strung with wire, key in a jar,
proved lightning was electricity, no mere star’s war.
Bifocals, stoves, catheter’s soft bend,
no patent he took—let the world share the end.

First loyal to crown, drew the snake split in two,
Join or Die, the first political call to renew.
Sent to London to speak for the colonies’ cause,
till the crown’s cold cruelty left him raw.
Leaked Hutchinson’s letters, shamed in the hall,
traded his loyalty for liberty’s call.

Sat with Jefferson to draft the great creed,
fixed “self-evident” where soft words had bleed.
Sailed for France, old and gray, seventy years,
wore fur caps, wined courtiers, calmed royal fears.
Secured the alliance that won the long fight,
brought peace home, the new nation’s first light.

Eighty-one at the Convention, carried through the door,
brokered the compromise that made union secure.
Shed his old sins, saw slavery’s deep stain,
led the fight to break every enslaved person’s chain.
Died in 1790, twenty thousand came to mourn,
a self-made man whose work is still borne.

On hundred-dollar bills, on library shelves, on every town’s street,
the first American—imperfect, complete.

Writing a good Chinese poem, whether classical or modern, hinges on balancing 3000 years of poetic tradition, the unique affordances of the Chinese language, and genuine personal voice. Below are core principles to guide your practice:
1. **Anchor in the foundational ethos of 言志缘情 (yán zhì yuán qíng, “express intent, root in emotion”)**
   The earliest preface to the *Classic of Poetry* (China’s oldest poetry collection) defines poetry as “the aim of the heart made verbal.” Before worrying about form or pretty language, identify the specific, lived feeling or conviction you want to convey, rather than leaning on generic sentiment (e.g., instead of vague “homesickness,” write of longing for the sound of your grandmother’s bamboo pestle pounding glutinous rice on Lunar New Year’s Eve). Authenticity matters more than performative erudition.
2. **Master form before bending it to your purpose**
   Chinese poetry spans two broad categories, each with distinct conventions:
   - *Classical poetry* (gushi old-style verse, lüshi regulated verse, jueju quatrains, ci song lyrics, qu arias): Learn core formal rules first: pingze (level/oblique tone patterns, where modern Mandarin’s first and second tones count as level, third and fourth as oblique for contemporary composition), rhyme schemes (use reference texts like *Pingshui Yun* for traditional pre-modern rhyme, or modern Mandarin rhyme for accessible new-style classical verse), and fixed cipai (tune patterns) for ci and qu. That said, rules serve emotion: Li Bai, often called the “Poet Immortal,” regularly broke regulated verse parallelism rules when the flow of his feeling demanded it, and his work is celebrated for this freedom.
   - *Modern Chinese free verse*: While it has no fixed metrics, lean into the inherent cadence of Chinese (whether Mandarin or a regional dialect): tonal contrast, the flexibility of monosyllabic characters, and the natural 2-3 character pause rhythm of spoken Chinese. Avoid forcing Western sentence structures that feel clunky or unidiomatic in Chinese.
3. **Cultivate 意境 (yìjìng, artistic conception) via evocation, not direct statement**
   Yijing—the fusion of concrete sensory scene, personal emotion, and layered implied meaning—is the most valued quality in Chinese poetics, and it relies on two traditional techniques:
   - 兴 (xìng, evocative association): Lead with a natural or everyday image that echoes your core emotion, rather than stating the emotion outright. Instead of writing “I am lonely after my friend left,” open with “The willow by the ferry dropped its last catkin” (willows have been tied to parting for 2000 years) to ground the feeling in tangible detail.
   - 留白 (liúbái, intentional empty space): Leave gaps for the reader to fill. Tang poet Wang Wei’s line “We return, as the mountain moss turns green with dusk” never explicitly names the quiet joy of a day spent with a friend, but the unstated feeling lingers far longer than a direct declaration would.
4. **Use cultural allusions and imagery mindfully, avoid clichés**
   Chinese poetry has a shared 3000-year lexicon of imagery and allusions: chrysanthemums for reclusion, wild geese for distant letters, the Miluo River for Qu Yuan’s loyal grief, and so on. These only work if you infuse them with personal meaning, rather than dropping them as empty decoration. For example, instead of the generic “I love chrysanthemums like Tao Yuanming,” write “I planted ten chrysanthemum seedlings by my balcony this spring / Only three bloomed—Tao Yuanming never had to deal with city smog” to twist a familiar allusion for modern lived experience. Prioritize plain, precise language over overly ornate, archaic phrasing; masters like Tao Yuanming and Bai Juyi used conversational, simple language to write some of the most beloved poems in the tradition.
5. **Revise for linguistic resonance**
   Every Chinese character carries layered connotations built from millennia of use, so cut any word that does not earn its place. Read your poem aloud to test flow: for classical verse, check that the pingze rhythm feels natural rather than forced; for free verse, confirm line breaks match the natural breathing rhythm of spoken Chinese.

P.S. If you are new to Chinese poetry, start small: first memorize 50–100 core works spanning the *Classic of Poetry*, Tang dynasty regulated verse, Song ci, and 20th-century free verse to internalize the tradition’s rhythm and imagery, then practice writing 4-line jueju or short free verse pieces rooted in small, mundane daily moments (a bowl of warm congee for breakfast, a rainstorm on the commute home) before tackling longer, allusion-heavy works. Many beginners fixate on archaic language or complex forms first, but the most moving Chinese poetry, regardless of era, is rooted in specific, genuine feeling rather than displays of scholarship.

# The Network We Built: Investing in *Wires and Waves: The Unruly History of the Internet*
On March 23, 2023, a 30-year-old TikTok CEO named Shou Zi Chew sat before a congressional committee that could barely explain how the app’s algorithm worked, much less the 50-year history of the network that made it possible. That hearing, which devolved into partisan talking points and uninformed questions about viral dance trends, summed up the global collective’s relationship to the internet: we spend more time on it than any other activity besides sleeping, we build our careers and our families and our identities around it, we fight to regulate it or protect it, but almost none of us know how it started, who built it, or what it was originally supposed to be. That gap in collective knowledge is the driving force behind *Wires and Waves: The Unruly History of the Internet*, a 108-minute feature documentary that will tell the full, unvarnished story of the most transformative invention of the 20th century, for the first time centering the unsung builders, activists, and everyday users who shaped the network, not just the billionaire founders who have become the public face of Silicon Valley. For potential investors, this film represents not just a chance to support a culturally significant work of nonfiction, but a low-risk, high-reward opportunity to tap into a massive, underserved audience hungry for nuanced, accessible context about the technology that defines every part of modern life.
Prior documentaries about the internet fall into three narrow, overdone categories: hagiographic profiles of celebrity CEOs that frame tech founders as uncomplicated geniuses, dry academic deep dives into coding and infrastructure that are inaccessible to general audiences, or alarmist takes that reduce the internet to a monolithic source of misinformation and mental harm. None of these films connect the internet’s countercultural 1960s origins to the urgent policy and cultural debates of 2024, and none of them center the voices of the people who were excluded from official histories: women, queer people, Black and Indigenous creators, and low-income users who turned the network into a lifeline long before it was a corporate profit center. Our director, Lila Marquez, a 32-year-old former Facebook content moderator and self-described “GeoCities teen,” came up with the idea for the film in 2020, after spending a 12-hour shift moderating election misinformation and realizing she had no idea how the tool she used every day had become so powerful, so fractured, and so unaccountable to the people who rely on it. Marquez spent five years researching hidden internet archives and tracking down unsung subjects before securing exclusive access to 120 hours of never-before-seen archival footage from the Internet Archive, including early chat room logs, GeoCities site recordings, 1990s webcam footage, and home videos from dot-com boom launch parties that no other documentary has ever licensed. The film is structured in three chronological acts, designed to feel propulsive and emotional, not educational or dry, with original animated segments from a BAFTA-nominated animation studio that explain technical concepts like packet switching and algorithmic recommendation in playful, accessible language, similar to the breakdowns in *The Big Short* but tailored to the internet’s weird, playful early energy.
Act 1 opens on the third floor of UCLA’s Boelter Hall on October 29, 1969, where 21-year-old grad student Charley Kline sat at a clunky SDS 940 computer, trying to send the first message between his UCLA ARPANET node and a second node 350 miles away at Stanford Research Institute. The message was supposed to be “LOGIN,” but the system crashed after just two letters: “LO,” a happy accident that Kline later joked was the most prophetic first message in human history, short for “Lo and behold.” What most official histories leave out is that Kline and his small team of grad students were not just doing contract work for the Department of Defense, which funded ARPANET as a Cold War communications tool designed to survive a nuclear attack; they were anti-war activists who saw the network as a way to share protest flyers and research across state lines without government interference, to build a community that transcended the violent political divisions of the Vietnam era. Act 1 also introduces audiences to Elizabeth Feinler, the 92-year-old former director of the Network Information Center, who ran the entire internet’s directory from a small office in Menlo Park in the 1970s and 1980s, invented the system of domain categories like .com, .org, and .edu, and was left out of nearly every official history of the internet until Marquez tracked her down for an exclusive 12-hour interview series in 2023. Feinler’s story is not just a fun, underdog side note; it is a microcosm of the internet’s core, defining contradiction: it was built by marginalized, underpaid people working for the public good, but its financial and cultural rewards would later be hoarded by a small group of wealthy, mostly male executives.
Act 2 moves into the 1990s, when the National Science Foundation lifted restrictions on commercial use of the internet, opening the door for the dot-com boom that would transform Silicon Valley from a quiet hub of research labs into the global center of wealth and power it is today. Instead of focusing solely on household names like Jeff Bezos and Mark Cuban, though, Act 2 centers the everyday users who turned the internet from a research tool into a global cultural phenomenon: the 16-year-old trans girl in rural Ohio who ran a GeoCities support group for queer youth in 1996, at a time when her hometown had zero in-person LGBTQ+ resources; the group of open-source activists who fought Microsoft’s attempt to monopolize web browsing in the late 1990s, laying the groundwork for the net neutrality fights of the 2010s; and Justin Hall, the 19-year-old college student who started the first blog in 1994, posting details of his personal life, his relationships, and his struggles with depression long before anyone had coined the term “influencer.” Hall’s story is a perfect throughline for the entire film, because he went from being a countercultural figure who believed radical online transparency would dismantle systemic inequality to a vocal critic of social media, who now works as a mental health advocate for people who have been harmed by the pressure to overshare online for profit. Act 2 also explores the first great moral panic of the internet era: the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which would have criminalized posting “obscene or indecent” content online, and the grassroots movement of internet users, activists, and small tech companies that fought back to defeat most of the bill, setting the precedent for the largely unregulated internet we have today.
Act 3, the film’s final and most urgent act, covers the years from 2008 to the present, a period when the internet shifted from a largely decentralized space for community building to a centralized ecosystem controlled by five giant corporations: Meta, Google, Amazon, TikTok, and Apple. We deliberately reject the easy, one-note approach of framing the modern internet as an unmitigated force for good or evil; instead, we show its radical duality, cutting between raw, user-generated footage of 2011 Arab Spring activists using Facebook to organize protests that toppled authoritarian regimes, and 2016 footage of Russian troll farms using the exact same platform to spread misinformation that sowed division in the U.S. presidential election. We interview a 26-year-old Syrian activist who now lives in Germany, who used Facebook to coordinate medical supply drops during the civil war, and who still believes the internet saved her life, even as she watches the same platform be used to demonize refugees across Europe. We also interview a former Facebook content moderator who left the job in 2019 after developing PTSD from watching 8 hours of violent footage every day, who now advocates for better working conditions and stricter content moderation policies for frontline tech workers. We sit down with a 19-year-old TikTok creator who has 2.3 million followers for her educational content about Native American history, who says the internet has given her a platform to reach millions of people that she never would have had access to as a queer Indigenous woman living on a reservation in rural South Dakota. We also talk to a group of parents in Texas who are suing Meta for harming their teenage daughters’ mental health through Instagram’s algorithmic promotion of eating disorder content, who say the internet has robbed them of the ability to protect their kids from unregulated corporate harm. The film ends not with a definitive answer about whether the internet is good or bad, but with a question posed directly to the audience: what do we want the internet to be for the next generation? That open, reflective ending is intentional, because it is designed to spark conversation, not shut it down, and it is the key to the film’s long-term cultural and commercial success.
For investors, the most critical question is not just whether this film is culturally important, but whether it will deliver a strong, reliable return on investment, and the data from audience research, comparable titles, and pre-existing partnerships overwhelmingly confirms that it will. First, the target audience for this film is massive, spanning every demographic group and level of tech literacy. According to 2024 Nielsen data, U.S. adults spend an average of 7 hours and 22 minutes online every day, more time than they spend watching linear TV, listening to music, or attending in-person events combined. A 2023 Pew Research Center poll found that 82% of U.S. adults say they have “little to no understanding” of how the internet was invented or who runs it, and 76% say they would watch a documentary that explained the internet’s history in an accessible, engaging way. That audience crosses generational lines: Gen Z and millennials, who make up 62% of all streaming documentary viewers, grew up with social media and are hungry for context about the tools that define their social lives, their careers, and their mental health. Gen X, who were the first generation to use the internet as young adults, have a strong nostalgia for the early days of AOL chat rooms, Napster, and MySpace, and will turn out in droves for content that revisits that era with accuracy and heart, rather than the mocking, ironic tone that most media uses to discuss early internet culture. Baby boomers, who make up 30% of theatrical documentary attendees, are curious about the technology that has transformed their relationships with their grandkids, their access to healthcare, and their retirement finances, and want to understand the debates about TikTok bans and social media regulation that dominate the nightly news. We also have a built-in, underserved niche audience of educators and policy makers: the College Board recently added a unit on internet history to its AP Computer Science Principles curriculum, and there is currently no feature-length documentary that meets the curriculum’s requirements, giving us a direct line to 15,000 high schools and 4,000 colleges across the United States.
Our distribution strategy is designed to maximize revenue across every possible window, while minimizing risk through pre-existing commitments and strategic partnerships. We will launch the film with a festival run at Sundance, SXSW, TIFF, and the Berlin International Film Festival, all of which our sales agent—who has represented 12 Oscar-nominated documentaries in the last decade—has identified as perfect fits for the film’s tone and cultural relevance. Festival runs generate critical acclaim and viral social media buzz, which we will amplify by hosting opening-night Q&As with Marquez, Feinler, Hall, and other subjects at every festival screening. We know from recent documentary hits like *Still: A Michael J. Fox Movie* and *Summer of Soul* that these Q&A sessions generate short-form viral clips on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and X that drive massive ticket and streaming viewership: *Still* generated 120 million views across social media from Q&A clips alone, leading to a 40% increase in streaming viewership in its first week on Apple TV+. After the festival run, we will do a limited theatrical release in 25 major U.S. markets, including New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Austin, and Chicago, with in-person Q&As at every opening night screening to keep the social media buzz going. Following the theatrical run, we will have a 90-day exclusive streaming window with a major platform; we are already in advanced talks with Netflix, Hulu, and Apple TV+, all of which have expressed strong interest in the film due to its broad audience appeal and timeliness, and have submitted preliminary presale offers that already cover 60% of our total production budget. After the streaming window, we will launch our educational distribution arm, which will license the film to high schools, colleges, libraries, and community organizations for 10 years, generating steady, passive revenue that most documentaries never tap into. We project that educational licensing alone will generate $1.2 million in revenue over the next decade, with additional revenue from public television broadcasts in the U.S., EU, and Southeast Asia, where demand for English-language tech content is growing rapidly.
We also have secured branded partnership commitments that will offset 22% of our production costs before we even premiere, including a $500,000 sponsorship from Mozilla, the makers of Firefox, who will promote the film to their 7 million monthly active users and host 50 free community screenings across the country as part of their national media literacy initiative. Our revenue projections are based on comparable recent documentaries, and are deliberately conservative by industry standards to avoid overpromising to investors. *The Social Dilemma*, a 2020 documentary about social media’s harms, grossed $15 million in global revenue on a $2 million production budget, delivering a 7.5x return on investment for its investors. *WeCrashed: The Rise and Fall of WeWork*, a 2022 documentary about the WeWork scandal, generated 11 million streams in its first month on Hulu, and grossed $18 million in total revenue across all windows. Our film has a broader scope and broader audience appeal than both of those films, because it is not limited to one specific issue or one company; it tells the full story of the internet, which touches every part of every person’s life, and we project an 8x return on investment within three years of release. We also have access to state and federal film tax incentives that will reduce your upfront risk by 30%: our production is based in California, which offers a 25% tax credit for documentary productions with budgets over $1 million, and we qualify for an additional 5% federal tax credit for films with a verified social impact component, which our media literacy partnership with the Electronic Frontier Foundation satisfies. What sets this film apart from every other investment opportunity you might be considering is its unmatched timeliness: we are at an unprecedented inflection point in the history of the internet, with debates about AI regulation, TikTok bans, net neutrality, and social media’s impact on children dominating every news cycle, every congressional hearing, and every dinner table conversation in the country. Audiences are tired of hot takes and 280-character arguments about these issues; they want context, they want nuance, and they want to understand how we got here so they can make informed decisions about where we go next. This film will not just entertain audiences for two hours; it will spark national conversation, it will be used in classrooms for decades, and it will become the definitive cultural record of the most transformative invention of the last 100 years. We have already raised 40% of our $2.5 million production budget from a group of impact investors in Silicon Valley, and we are seeking $1.5 million in additional funding to complete principal photography, finish post-production, and launch our distribution and marketing campaigns. Every investor will receive a “Producer” credit in the film, access to exclusive premiere and festival events, and monthly updates on the film’s progress through every stage of production and distribution. We are not just asking for your capital; we are asking you to join us in telling a story that has never been told, that needs to be told now, and that will resonate with millions of people around the world for years to come.

Hey friends! Let’s start with a quick show of hands: who loves jumping in crunchy leaf piles in fall? Building snow forts and sipping hot cocoa after sledding in winter? Hunting for tiny flower buds and baby bunnies in spring? Or spending all afternoon at the pool eating blue popsicles in summer? Yeah, me too! Have you ever wondered why we get these four awesome, totally different seasons every year?

First, let’s bust a super common myth: it’s NOT because Earth gets closer to the sun for summer and farther away for winter! That tricked me when I was your age, too. Actually, when we’re having summer here in the U.S., Earth is a tiny bit FARTHER from the sun than it is in our winter. Wild, right?

The real secret is that Earth is tilted! Think of Earth like a big, squishy bouncy ball with a popsicle stick stuck straight through it, from the very top (that’s the North Pole, where Santa lives!) to the very bottom (the South Pole, where penguins hang out). That popsicle stick is what we spin around every single day to make day and night. But here’s the key: that popsicle stick is not straight up and down! It’s always tilted just a little bit—about as much as you’d tilt your head when you’re leaning in to hear a secret. And no matter where Earth goes as it loops around the sun (that trip takes 365 whole days, or one full year!), that tilt never changes direction. It’s always pointing the same way, like if you hold a tilted pencil and walk around a lamp in your bedroom, the top of the pencil always points at your closet door the whole time.

Now let’s talk about sunlight, because that’s what makes things warm! Grab a flashlight in your mind: if you point it straight at your palm, the light is super bright, tight, and warm, right? But if you tilt the flashlight so the light spreads out over your whole arm and part of your desk, it’s dimmer and not warm at all. That’s exactly how the sun’s light works on Earth.

When our half of Earth (the top half, where we live) is tilted TOWARD the sun as we loop around it, the sun’s light hits us straight on, like the flashlight on your palm. The light is all concentrated and cozy, and we get way more hours of sunlight too—so you get to play outside longer after school! That’s summer.

Half a year later, when Earth has moved to the opposite side of the sun, our half is tilted AWAY from the sun. Now the sun’s light hits us all spread out, like the tilted flashlight on your arm. It’s not as warm, and we get way fewer hours of sunlight—so it gets dark super early, and sometimes it snows! That’s winter.

Spring and fall are the in-between times, when we’re moving from one side of the sun to the other. Our tilt isn’t pointing straight toward or away from the sun, so the sunlight is halfway between concentrated and spread out. Days and nights are almost the same length, and the weather is nice and mild—perfect for planting flowers or picking pumpkins!

One super fun bonus fact: if you live on the bottom half of Earth, like in Australia, their seasons are flipped! When we’re building snowmen in December, they’re having pool parties for Christmas, because their half of Earth is tilted toward the sun when ours is tilted away. Cool, right?

P.S. Want to prove this yourself tonight with a super easy experiment? Grab a grown-up, a flashlight, a tennis ball (or even an orange or a bouncy ball!), and a marker. Draw a tiny smiley face on the top half of the ball—that’s you! Tilt the ball a little to one side, and keep it tilted the EXACT same way the whole time (no wiggling the tilt!). Have your grown-up hold the turned-on flashlight in the middle of the room—that’s the sun. Now walk in a big slow circle around the flashlight, holding your tilted smiley ball. Notice when the smiley face is tilted right toward the light (that’s summer for you!) and when it’s tilted away (that’s winter!). You don’t have to move closer or farther from the flashlight at all—just the tilt does all the work! Bonus silly fact: if Earth didn’t have that little tilt, we’d never have seasons ever. Every single day would be the same boring, mild temperature, no snow days, no pool days, no leaf piles. Yawn, right?
