# Loading Screen Lullaby
The blue glow of the loading screen hums to life when I slump into the couch after a long, draining day.
No one asks me to answer emails or fold the laundry or explain why I’m too tired to make small talk the second I press “start.”
The first pro is the *pixelated safe harbor* that wraps around me like a well-loved hoodie, sharp edges of the real world softening at the edges of my monitor.
I can be a dragon slayer in a mossy castle, a farmer tending to turnip patches on a distant moon, or a spaceship captain charting routes through asteroid belts no human has ever seen.
These roles don’t come with the pressure of real-world mistakes, because a failed boss fight just means I respawn thirty seconds back, no harm done, no apologies needed.
I’ve learned *low-stakes problem-solving* that sneaks into my daily life, too: the pattern recognition that lets me spot a glitch in a work spreadsheet the same way I spot a boss’s weak point mid-battle.
The multitasking I honed juggling healing spells and map navigation makes it easier to juggle grocery lists and appointment reminders when I’m off the couch.
I’ve met people who live three thousand miles away, people who get my dumb inside jokes about hidden chests and speedrun glitches, who stay up with me to grind through a tough raid when my real-life friends are busy.
This *global found family* has brought me soup when I had COVID, celebrated my graduation over voice chat, and held space for my grief when my grandma died, all because we first bonded over a shared love of a silly farming sim.
Video games let me practice courage in small, measurable ways: facing a terrifying horror game demon at 9 p.m. makes it easier to face a scary work presentation at 9 a.m. the next day.
They spark creativity, too: I’ve written fanfiction about my favorite characters, drawn fan art of the rolling, flower-dusted landscapes I’ve explored, and even taught myself basic coding to mod my favorite indie game to add a fluffy calico cat sidekick.
For hours at a time, I can forget that I’m anxious or tired or overwhelmed, because my brain is fully focused on a goal that feels entirely within my control.
That focus is a gift, one I rarely find scrolling social media or watching mindless television, where my attention drifts every two minutes to the growing list of tasks I haven’t finished.
But for every bright, glowing pro, there is a con that creeps in quiet, uninvited, when I finally look up from the screen and realize the sun has dipped below the horizon without me noticing.
The first con is the *blue light brain fog* that settles thick behind my eyes after four hours straight of staring at the monitor, making it hard to read a physical book or hold a face-to-face conversation without zoning out mid-sentence.
My wrists ache from holding the controller too tight, my shoulders hunch so high they brush my ears, and I have to remind myself to stand up and stretch long after the stiffness has settled deep into my muscles.
I’ve missed so many small, perfect real-world moments because I was too busy chasing a virtual achievement: my niece’s first wobbly steps across the living room rug, my mom’s famous chocolate chip cookies coming out of the oven still steaming, a thunderstorm that painted the sunset sky streaks of tangerine and lavender right outside my bedroom window.
Those *unread text threads* piling up on my lock screen are proof of the connections I let slip because I was too wrapped up in a virtual world to answer a friend asking to get iced coffee and walk around the lake.
I’ve stayed up until 3 a.m. chasing a final boss’s second phase, only to drag myself through work the next day, running on two hours of sleep and a lukewarm vanilla latte, too tired to enjoy the real life I’ve worked so hard to build.
The line between virtual stress and real stress starts to blur after a while: a bad loss in a competitive ranked match can leave me snappy and irritable for hours, as if I’d actually failed at something that matters beyond the server’s shutdown notice.
I’ve spent $40 on cosmetic skins for a character I’ll play for three months tops, money that could have gone to a new poetry collection or a dinner out with my sister or a donation to the food bank three blocks from my apartment.
The *quiet grief of missed sunsets* nags at me when I finally log off, realizing I spent the entire beautiful, sun-drenched Saturday inside, not feeling the warm grass under my feet or the breeze on my cheeks.
Sometimes I catch myself daydreaming about respawning in real life, about being able to redo an awkward conversation or a bad work day the same way I can redo a failed level, and that’s when I know I’ve spent too much time in a world where mistakes don’t leave permanent marks.
Video games don’t remind you to drink water or take your allergy meds or call your dad on his birthday, so those small, essential tasks fall by the wayside when I’m deep in a story campaign, leaving me scrambling to catch up when I finally surface from the screen’s glow.
I’ve had arguments with my partner about how much time I spend glued to the monitor, how I zone out when they’re talking to me mid-quest, how I cancel picnic plans last minute because I’m too close to finishing a game to hit pause.
The virtual friends I love so much can sometimes feel like a lazy replacement for the real people sitting right next to me, even though a voice chat “I’m sorry” can never replace a tight, warm hug when I’m actually heartbroken.
Those *virtual wins that leave no physical trophy* feel hollow sometimes, when I look around my apartment and realize I have dozens of platinum achievements saved to my account but no printed photos of me hiking with friends or baking with my mom to hang on my fridge.
I’ve forgotten how to sit with silence, how to just be bored without grabbing a controller or booting up a game, because the constant stimulation of virtual worlds makes quiet, unstructured time feel empty and uncomfortable.
My eyes have gotten worse over the years, the eye doctor telling me I need to take twenty-minute breaks every hour to look at something twenty feet away, a rule I almost never follow when I’m in the middle of a gut-wrenching story twist.
I’ve eaten so many cold, half-eaten bags of cheddar chips and microwave burritos over my keyboard, meals I barely tasted because I was too focused on a cutscene to pay attention to what I was putting in my body.
But even with all these sharp, heavy cons, I can’t bring myself to write off video games entirely, because they’ve given me too much that the real world never could when I needed it most.
They gave me a place to be myself when I was a closeted teen, too scared to talk to anyone at school about who I really was, because my online friends didn’t care what I looked like or who I loved, only how good I was at healing the party during tough raids.
They gave me a reason to get out of bed on my worst depression days, when even brushing my teeth felt like an impossible task, because I knew my in-game farm needed me to water the strawberry crops and my friends were waiting for me to log on to play our weekly trivia game.
They taught me that failure isn’t the end of the world, that trying again and again until you get it right is just part of the process, a lesson I’ve carried with me through every nerve-wracking job interview and every hard, tearful conversation I’ve ever had.
The trick, I’ve learned after years of swinging between binge-playing and guilt-fueled breaks, is to hold both the pros and the cons gently, without judging myself too harshly for loving something that has messy, noticeable flaws.
I can set a timer on my phone to remind myself to stand up every hour, to log off by 11 p.m. so I get enough sleep, to put the controller down the second my niece knocks on my door to show me her new crayon drawing.
I can plan in-person game nights with my real-life friends, passing controllers around the coffee table and eating greasy pepperoni pizza together, blending the virtual and the real instead of letting them pull me in opposite directions.
I can save my cosmetic skin money for one small treat a month, and put the rest toward the real-world adventures I want to have, like a weekend trip to the coast or a pottery class with my best friend from high school.
The *balance that never quite feels like enough* is still worth chasing, because video games don’t have to be an escape from my life, they can be a joyful part of it, as long as I don’t let them take over the parts that matter most.
I still get that giddy, childlike thrill when the loading screen pops up, when I hear the familiar, cozy theme song of my favorite farming sim, when my friends log on and yell silly greetings down the voice chat line.
I still feel that small, familiar twinge of guilt when I realize I’ve spent too long playing, when I see the moon high in the sky and I haven’t left the house all day.
But that messy mix of joy and guilt, of connection and distance, of wild adventure and quiet stillness, is just part of loving something that lives both on a glowing screen and in the soft, messy, perfect parts of my real life.

- Generative Adversarial Networks are a machine learning architecture composed of two competing neural networks
- The two core networks are called the generator and the discriminator
- The generator learns to create synthetic data that matches patterns from real training datasets
- The discriminator acts as a binary classifier to distinguish real data from fake generated data
- The two networks train simultaneously in a competitive zero sum game framework
- Early GAN training often faces the issue of lacking coherent or realistic output details
- The generator updates its parameters whenever the discriminator correctly identifies its output as fake
- The discriminator updates its parameters whenever it misclassifies real or generated data
- A fully trained high functioning GAN can produce synthetic data of exceptional quality that is nearly indistinguishable from real data
- Each custom GAN model is often built for a specific use case such as image generation or voice synthesis
- Careful hyperparameter tuning and training monitoring are required to maintain reliable GAN performance across use cases
P.P.S GANs are applied across many fields including entertainment healthcare and synthetic data generation for other AI systems

Unlike much harsher acids like HYDROCHLORIC ACID that can eat through healthy, unrusted steel if left on even for a few minutes, the phosphoric acid in regular Coke is diluted enough that it won’t immediately damage the steel of your chain during short exposures, which is why this DIY hack has spread so widely across social media and household cleaning forums. STEEL WOOL is also a moderately effective abrasive for this specific job, as its fine, sharp edges can scrape away loosened rust particles without immediately gouging the smooth metal surfaces of the chain links that are critical for smooth, friction-free pedaling. The first step of paying taxes centers on gathering all required financial documentation and using that data to calculate your official tax liability for the year. Start by compiling all income-related forms: W-2s from full- or part-time employers, 1099s for freelance, gig, investment, or rental income, 1098s for student loan interest or mortgage payments, and receipts for any eligible deductible expenses, such as charitable donations, out-of-pocket medical costs exceeding 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, educator classroom supplies, or contributions to a traditional IRA. Next, sum all taxable earnings to find your gross income, then subtract above-the-line deductions (deductions you can claim without itemizing) to get your adjusted gross income, or AGI. From there, subtract either the standard deduction (a fixed, inflation-adjusted amount based on your filing status: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, or head of household) or the total of your itemized deductions, whichever reduces your taxable income more. Finally, apply current year IRS tax brackets to your taxable income to find your pre-credit tax liability, then subtract any eligible tax credits (like the Child Tax Credit, Earned Income Tax Credit, or residential energy credits) and any taxes you already paid during the year via payroll withholding or quarterly estimated payments. The resulting number will tell you if you owe additional taxes or are eligible for a refund.
***
Once you have finalized your liability calculations, the next step is to file your tax return with the appropriate federal and state tax agencies by the annual deadline, typically April 15, unless the date falls on a weekend or federal holiday, or you request a 6-month filing extension. You have several options to file: free electronic filing via IRS Free File, which is available to all taxpayers with an annual AGI of $79,000 or less as of 2024 and walks you through the process step-by-step; paid tax software for more complex returns; a certified tax preparer, such as a CPA or enrolled agent, for high-income, self-employed, or otherwise complicated tax situations; or free in-person assistance via Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) or Tax Counseling for the Elderly (TCE) programs for low-income, disabled, or senior filers. Most filers will use Form 1040 for federal taxes, with additional supporting schedules if you have itemized deductions, self-employment income, capital gains, or other specialized tax situations. Before submitting, double-check that all personal information, including Social Security numbers for you, your spouse, and any dependents, your mailing address, and your bank account details for direct deposit or electronic payment, is accurate, as errors can cause weeks of processing delays. If you owe taxes, you can pay via direct bank transfer, credit or debit card, a monthly payment plan, or a check mailed with your return, and note that a filing extension only extends the deadline to submit your return, not the deadline to pay any owed taxes.
***
After you submit your return and any required payment, there are a few final steps to complete to wrap up the process and prepare for future tax years. First, save a complete copy of your filed return, all supporting forms (W-2s, 1099s, receipts), and proof of payment for 3 to 7 years, depending on your situation, as the IRS can audit returns within this window if discrepancies or red flags appear. # The 2AM Production Riddle Only Senior Devs Solve On The First Try

It’s 2:17 AM. Your Slack notifications blare like a server closet smoke alarm. PagerDuty hit your phone so hard it slid off your nightstand. The e-commerce checkout pipeline is down, Black Friday starts in 4 hours, and your CTO just replied to the outage thread with a single :panic_parrot: emoji. Before you ssh into the cluster, bleary-eyed enough to typo sudo as suod three times in a row, let me hit you with a riddle more accurate to your job than any LeetCode hard you’ve grinded on a Sunday:

I have a name but no birth certificate, a parent that abandons me before I breathe.
I eat resources but never ask for seconds, I hide in plain sight but no process list will let you see.
I outlive my creator, ignore all kill signals, haunt the same PID namespace till the node finally bleeds.
What am I?

Before you fire off a guess in the comments, let’s eliminate the obvious (and very tempting) red herrings with three clues tailored to anyone who’s ever stared at a top output for 45 minutes straight:

Clue 1: I’m not a junior dev on their first on-call shift. Yes, I ignore all forms of communication, outlast my manager’s tenure by 18 months, and waste cloud resources that get billed to a team I’ve never even met. But unlike a junior, I never accidentally merge straight to main at 3AM while hopped up on energy drinks. (Mostly because I don’t have hands. Or a GitHub account.)
Clue 2: I’m not a Kubernetes Pod stuck in a taint-tolerated namespace. Yes, I have a parent that abandons me mid-execution (shoutout to kubelet crashing right as it was supposed to terminate a ReplicaSet), I eat CPU and memory like free office matcha lattes, and I stick around long after the Deployment that spawned me was deleted in a fit of “spring cleaning.” But pods have YAML manifests to call their own. I don’t even get a half-baked config file with 12 deprecated fields.
Clue 3: I’m not the uncommented regular expression your staff engineer wrote in 2019 to validate coupon codes. Yes, no one alive knows how I work, no one dares kill me lest the entire payments system collapse, and I’ve outlasted three company reorgs and two full frontend rewrites. But regexes at least have a 2014 Stack Overflow thread that sort of explains their logic. I don’t even show up in top output half the time if you forget to run it with the right flags.

If you guessed zombie process, ding ding ding! You’ve either spent way too much time debugging bare-metal Linux boxes, or you just have a very specific trauma related to the wait() syscall. For anyone who’s never had the joy of hunting these gremlins: zombie processes are dead child processes whose parent exited without calling wait() to clean up their entry in the process table. They don’t actually eat CPU or memory, but they hog PID slots until their grandparent init process finally reaps them— or, more likely, until you give up and reboot the whole node at 3AM because you can’t be bothered to track down the missing SIGCHLD handler.

The punchline? We ran this riddle past 42 engineers in our Slack last week while waiting for a CI build to finish, and 68% of mid-level devs guessed “Kubernetes pod” or “that one broken Lambda that only fails on Tuesdays.” We’re so conditioned to chase complex, shiny, resume-worthy problems—race conditions in distributed caches, misconfigured IAM roles, GraphQL schema collisions—that we forget the boring, 40-year-old Unix quirks that still break production more often than any cloud-native disaster.

We spend hundreds of hours learning distributed systems design and cloud architecture, but half of production outages still boil down to “someone forgot a basic syscall” or “there’s 200 dead processes hogging all the PID slots.” It’s the most humbling part of this job: no matter how fancy your stack gets, the basics always come back to bite you.

Now go fix that checkout pipeline. And check for zombies first. You’re welcome.

The statement “Wizards are more powerful than sorcerers because they study magic instead of being born with it” is a pervasive, often oversimplified take that crops up most frequently in [tabletop role-playing game community Discord servers], though it also pops up in fantasy media discourse and even casual fan debates at [local genre book club meetups]. At its core, the claim relies on two flawed assumptions: first, that deliberate study of magic inherently produces greater raw or practical power than innate magical affinity, and second, that all magic systems across all works of fantasy operate by the same rules that govern the most popular TTRPG iterations of these classes. To unpack the first flaw, it’s useful to ground the discussion in 5th Edition Dungeons & Dragons, the system where this debate is most commonly waged, since it codifies wizards as Intelligence-based, spellbook-reliant casters and sorcerers as Charisma-based casters with innate magical roots tied to bloodlines, wild magic surges, or divine blessings. Wizards do have undeniable advantages that lend credence to the claim at first glance: they can copy nearly any spell from scrolls or other wizards’ spellbooks into their own, giving them access to a far wider pool of potential spells than sorcerers, who are locked into a much smaller, fixed list of spells known once they level up. This versatility means a wizard who has time to prepare for a specific encounter can tailor their spell loadout to exploit an enemy’s weaknesses, stock up on utility spells for out-of-combat problem-solving, and even swap out low-impact spells for more relevant ones between long rests. But this advantage is heavily dependent on context, and it falls apart in scenarios where preparation time is limited, resources are scarce, or the party needs a caster who can adapt quickly to chaotic, unforeseen circumstances in the middle of a fight. Sorcerers, by contrast, have access to metamagic, a unique class feature that lets them modify spells on the fly to fit the situation: they can cast a spell silently to sneak past guards, extend the range of a healing spell to reach a downed ally across the battlefield, or twin a buff spell to affect two party members instead of one, all without needing to plan for those modifications ahead of time. This flexibility is especially valuable in [low-level one-shot campaigns] where players don’t have time to accumulate a large library of spells or scrolls, because a sorcerer can make the most of the few spells they do know in ways a wizard simply cannot. The second core flaw of the statement is that it treats “power” as a single, universal metric, when in reality, power in fantasy settings is almost always defined by the specific goal a caster is trying to achieve, the context they are operating in, and the constraints of the world they live in. For example, in a [custom homebrew magic system] where innate magical ability is tied to the capacity to channel raw, unfiltered magical energy from the fabric of the universe, a sorcerer might be capable of feats of raw destructive power that no wizard, no matter how many decades they spend studying, could ever replicate, simply because their bodies are built to handle that level of magical strain. Conversely, in a setting where magic is a precise, formulaic practice that requires exacting knowledge of arcane symbols and ancient incantations, a wizard’s rigorous study would give them an edge in casting complex, ritualistic spells that a sorcerer’s innate, intuitive grasp of magic might not be able to replicate without years of supplementary training. It ignores the fact that many sorcerers in lore do study magic, even if they are born with a core of innate power: a sorcerer with a wild magic bloodline might spend years learning to control their surges to avoid hurting the people around them, while a sorcerer descended from a celestial being might train extensively to master the healing magic that runs in their family. Similarly, many wizards have innate advantages that make their study possible, whether that’s a natural aptitude for arcane theory, access to expensive spellbooks and materials from a young age, or a mentor who can guide them through the earliest, most dangerous stages of magical training. To reduce the entire complex dynamic between these two caster archetypes to “study beats innate talent” erases all of this nuance, and it also fails to account for how player choice and build creativity can shift the power dynamic entirely. A min-maxed sorcerer built to specialize in area-of-effect damage, for example, can outpace a poorly built wizard focused on niche, low-impact utility spells in almost every combat scenario, even if the wizard has spent far more in-game time studying their spellbook. The debate also shifts dramatically when you move beyond TTRPGs to other fantasy media, where the definitions of wizard and sorcerer can vary wildly from one franchise to the next. In [popular 1990s fantasy novel series], for example, sorcerers are the only casters capable of accessing the deepest layers of the magical realm, while wizards are limited to surface-level, ritualistic magic that pales in comparison to the raw, reality-bending power sorcerers can wield with barely a thought. Meanwhile, in [urban fantasy television show that ran from 2012 to 2019], wizards are born with magical ability just like sorcerers, but they choose to study formal magic theory to refine their craft, while sorcerers rely on instinct and often struggle to control their power during high-stress situations, leading to a more nuanced dynamic where neither is inherently more powerful, just better suited to different tasks. To make a broad, universal claim about one being more powerful than the other ignores all of these franchise-specific differences, and it also ignores the personal preferences of players and creators who might prioritize different types of power when building their characters or worlds. For example, a player who values storytelling and role-play over raw combat power might consider a sorcerer more powerful because their innate magic comes with a rich backstory tied to their bloodline or a life-altering magical event, while a player who loves problem-solving and preparation might find wizards more powerful for their ability to outthink encounters before they even start. To illustrate just how context-dependent this debate really is, let’s break down two specific scenarios where the core claim of the statement either holds true or falls apart completely:
* The claim that wizards are more powerful due to study holds most true in [high-stakes endgame boss fights] where the party has weeks of in-game time to prepare, access to a fully stocked arcane library, and advance knowledge of the boss’s weaknesses and resistances. In these scenarios, a wizard can copy specific counterspells, damage spells that exploit the boss’s elemental weakness, and utility spells that neutralize the boss’s most dangerous abilities into their spellbook, prepare their entire loadout around the fight, and even craft custom magic items to boost their capabilities before the battle even begins. A sorcerer, by contrast, would be limited to their small list of known spells, and while they could use metamagic to modify those spells, they would not be able to access the wide range of specialized spells a wizard could pull from their spellbook to tailor their approach perfectly to the fight. Even here, though, the wizard’s advantage relies entirely on having access to those preparation resources: if the party is ambushed by the same boss with no advance warning, the sorcerer’s ability to adapt on the fly could easily be more valuable than the wizard’s loadout of spells prepared for a completely different set of circumstances.
* The claim falls apart almost entirely in narrative-focused campaigns set in [rural village under a fey curse] where resources are scarce, information is unreliable, and the party is forced to make split-second decisions with long-term consequences for the people they are trying to protect. In this setting, a wizard would struggle to find the rare ink, parchment, and scrolls they need to copy new spells into their book, and they would have no way to research the specific rules of the fey curse in advance, since local records are spotty and the fey guarding the village intentionally spread misinformation about how their magic works. A sorcerer with a fey wild magic bloodline, by contrast, would have an innate intuitive understanding of fey magic that would let them recognize loopholes in the curse, communicate with the fey guardians without accidentally triggering a binding oath, and even channel their innate magic to temporarily suppress the curse’s effects on individual villagers long enough to evacuate them to safety. This type of contextual power, which is tied to alignment with the setting’s core magical rules, is far more impactful than any power gained through study, and it is something no amount of wizardly research could replicate without the sorcerer’s innate connection to the specific type of magic at play.

The idea that hard work and study can overcome innate talent is a comforting narrative that aligns with many people’s real-world values, so they project that narrative onto fantasy caster archetypes even when the lore or rules of the setting don’t support it. But this projection often erases the work that sorcerers put into mastering their power, as well as the innate advantages that many wizards have that let them pursue their study in the first place. For example, a wizard born into a wealthy noble family who can afford to pay for a top-tier arcane education, a private tutor, and a steady supply of rare spell components has a massive advantage over a sorcerer born into poverty who has to teach themselves to control their power while working 12-hour shifts at [dockside tavern in a port city] to pay for food and shelter, even if the sorcerer’s raw magical potential is far higher. The statement’s framing of study as a choice that makes wizards more worthy of power also ignores the fact that many sorcerers never asked for their innate magic, and many wizards choose to study magic because they have no innate talent for it, making their study a necessity rather than a mark of superior dedication. It’s also worth noting that many fantasy settings blur the line between wizards and sorcerers entirely, with casters who have both innate magical ability and years of formal study, making the entire distinction meaningless in those contexts. At the end of the day, the question of whether wizards are more powerful than sorcerers is not one that has a universal answer, because power is too subjective, too context-dependent, and too tied to the specific rules and lore of the setting where the question is being asked. The statement’s attempt to boil that complex question down to a simple binary of study vs innate talent does a disservice to the creativity and nuance that make fantasy magic systems so engaging for fans around the world. Instead of debating which archetype is inherently more powerful, fans and players are better off exploring the unique strengths that each brings to a story or campaign, and the ways their different approaches to magic can complement each other when they work together toward a common goal. A wizard and a sorcerer traveling together can combine the wizard’s vast library of specialized spells and arcane knowledge with the sorcerer’s ability to adapt those spells to unforeseen circumstances, creating a team that is far more powerful than either could ever be on their own. This collaborative dynamic is often far more interesting and narratively satisfying than any arbitrary ranking of power based on how a character gained their magic, and it opens up far more opportunities for compelling storytelling and character development. Whether you prefer the studious, preparation-focused approach of a wizard or the intuitive, adaptable approach of a sorcerer, the most important thing is that the character feels meaningful to you, and that their approach to magic fits the story you want to tell, whether that story is a casual one-shot with friends, a years-long TTRPG campaign, or a novel you’re writing for [independent fantasy publishing press]. Next time you see this debate pop up in a comment section or a casual conversation, it’s worth pushing back on the oversimplified framing of study as inherently superior to innate talent, because that framing erases so much of the nuance that makes fantasy magic feel magical in the first place.

<<Two Companions Of Pine Edge Cottage>>
I live in a small cedar cottage tucked between a thick pine forest and a rolling meadow. I adopted my dog from a local animal shelter four years ago. He was a lanky nervous puppy who hid behind the shelter kennel bed when I first approached. My dog is brown and my cat is black. The dog’s fur carries the deep warm tone of dried pine bark left out in summer sun. I named him Bramble for his tendency to run straight through thorny blackberry patches on walks. He loves to carry large smooth sticks back to the cottage from our daily treks through the woods. He curls on the wool rug beside my desk while I work on cold winter afternoons.
I found my cat huddled under my back porch step during a heavy rainstorm two years later. She was a tiny undernourished kitten with matted fur and a quiet mew. Her fur holds the rich inky shade of a moonless night sky over the forest. I named her Shadow for her habit of following me from room to room without making a sound. She likes to nap on the wooden windowsill above the kitchen sink. She bats at stray dandelion seeds that drift past the glass on soft spring breezes.
Bramble and Shadow formed a close bond within days of Shadow moving into the cottage. Bramble lets Shadow curl on his thick furry belly during afternoon naps. Shadow grooms the fur between Bramble’s ears after he comes inside muddy from long walks. They sit side by side at the front gate each evening to wait for me to return from trips to the town general store. Local children often stop to wave at the pair when they walk past the cottage on their way to the meadow. The bright brown shape and deep black shape make a striking contrast against the pale wooden fence that lines my property.
Visitors to the cottage almost always comment on the two animals first. They ask how the pair came to live with me. I tell them each found their way to my home in their own time. I say they bring more joy to my days than I ever thought possible. They are the steady quiet heart of my small life at the edge of the woods.

Congratulations on your new puppy—such a fun (and sometimes chaotic!) milestone! All the options below are humane, age-appropriate for young puppies, and tailored to first-time owners:

1. Self-Guided Positive Reinforcement Training: This beginner-friendly, reward-based method focuses on immediately rewarding desired behaviors (like going potty outside, sitting calmly, or nipping toys instead of hands) with high-value treats, praise, or play, instead of scolding mistakes. You’ll do 5-10 minute daily sessions (perfect for a puppy’s short attention span) to teach core cues (sit, stay, come) and build consistent potty/crate training routines. There are tons of free, vetted resources (like certified trainer guides from the ASPCA or beginner-friendly training TikTok accounts) to walk you through each step, and this method prioritizes building trust and bonding with your puppy. It’s ideal if you’re on a budget, have a flexible schedule, and prefer learning at your own pace.

2. Structured Puppy Group Classes: Led by certified professional dog trainers, these 4-6 week weekly classes are designed for puppies 8-16 weeks old (the critical socialization window). Each session combines basic cue training, supervised off-leash play to teach bite inhibition and polite interaction with other dogs and people, and dedicated Q&A time for your specific struggles (like midnight potty accidents or chewing shoes). The hands-on guidance lets a trainer correct your technique in real time, and the built-in socialization helps prevent fear or aggression issues as your puppy grows. This is a great pick if you learn best with in-person support, want to check off critical socialization, and connect with other new puppy owners.

3. In-Home Private One-on-One Training: With this option, a certified trainer comes directly to your home to build a fully personalized training plan tailored to your puppy’s unique quirks and your lifestyle. They can address specific early issues that group classes might not cover, like separation anxiety, extreme nipping, or potty training struggles in apartments without yards, and will adjust training to fit your household (for example, if you have young kids or other pets). They’ll also help you set up daily routines that fit your work or family schedule. This is ideal if you have specific, urgent training concerns, a busy schedule that can’t accommodate group classes, or want fully customized guidance.

Which one you choose?

One of the most widespread uses of poppy seeds is in sweet baked goods, where their subtle nutty flavor and satisfying crunchy texture elevate dishes across European, Middle Eastern, and North African cuisines. Blue poppy seeds, the most common variety in Western baking, are studded on bagels, muffins, and danishes, or ground into creamy fillings for Austrian poppy seed strudel, Polish makowiec, and Jewish hamantaschen cookies served during Purim. White poppy seeds, by contrast, are often preferred for lighter baked goods where their pale color won’t alter the final appearance, and they are frequently soaked in milk or sugar syrup to soften their texture before being blended into fillings for cakes and pastries.


Beyond sweet preparations, poppy seeds are a versatile staple in savory cooking, particularly in South Asian and Mediterranean culinary traditions. In Indian cuisine, where they are known as khus khus, white poppy seeds are often toasted and ground into a fine paste that acts as a dairy-free thickener for rich curries, kormas, and biryani sauces, adding a silky mouthfeel and depth of flavor without overwhelming other spices. Across Turkey, Greece, and the Balkans, whole poppy seeds are sprinkled on savory flatbreads like pide and lavash, mixed into herbaceous salad dressings, or added to meat rubs for roasted lamb and chicken, lending a delicate, earthy contrast to bold, savory notes.


Poppy seeds and their derived oil also have a long history of use in traditional medicinal systems around the world. In Ayurveda, the traditional medicine of India, poppy seeds are valued for their mild sedative and cooling properties, often mixed with warm milk, honey, and a pinch of nutmeg as a natural remedy for insomnia, anxiety, and restlessness. European folk medicine has similarly used poppy seed infusions to soothe irritated throats, suppress persistent coughs, and ease mild digestive discomfort like bloating and cramping, though modern medical practitioners note these effects are mild, and edible poppy seeds contain only trace amounts of the opiate alkaloids found in other parts of the opium poppy plant.


In the personal care and cosmetic industry, poppy seeds and cold-pressed poppy seed oil are prized for their nourishing, gentle properties suitable for sensitive skin and hair. Whole poppy seeds act as a natural, non-irritating exfoliant in facial scrubs, body washes, and lip polishes, sloughing away dead skin cells without causing micro-tears in delicate skin tissue. Cold-pressed poppy seed oil is high in linoleic acid, antioxidants, and vitamin E, making it a popular ingredient in moisturizers, hair serums, and lip balms; its non-comedogenic nature means it won’t clog pores, making it ideal for acne-prone and dry skin types alike.


Poppy seeds also play key roles in sustainable agricultural and livestock systems, extending far beyond direct human use. Poppy plants grown for seed production produce large, nectar-rich flowers that are a critical food source for native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies, boosting pollinator populations and increasing pollination rates for adjacent fruit and vegetable crops. * Digitally native workflows that have cut case backlogs by 32% in the first 12 pilot areas. Gone are the days of magistrates hauling 50-pound paper binders into court, cross-referencing handwritten police notes and outdated case records mid-hearing. The new magistracy is issued secure, encrypted tablets preloaded with real-time police data, social service records, and pre-vetted support resource directories, cutting down hearing times by an average of 22 minutes per case. The new cohort is 41% under 40, 34% from racially minoritized backgrounds, and includes youth workers, freelance graphic designers, primary school teachers, and former care leavers, rather than the traditional pool of lawyers and local business owners. A 2023 impact report found that 68% of defendants said they felt their personal circumstances were taken into account under the new system, compared to 32% in 2020.

The old magistracy relied heavily on one-size-fits-all fines and short custodial sentences that often trapped people in cycles of debt and reoffense. The new magistrates are trained to prioritize tailored, non-punitive resolutions for first-time and low-level offenders: connecting a single parent who shoplifted baby formula to emergency food grants and benefits advocacy, assigning a teen caught vandalizing a local park to a 10-week community art program instead of a criminal record, and waiving court fees for people living below the poverty line.

I got to see this new system in action last month, sitting in on a day of hearings at a magistrates court in South London. The room was bright, no stuffy oak paneling or wigs in sight—magistrates wore smart, neutral business attire, and defendants were invited to sit at a table with their support workers instead of standing in a raised, intimidating dock. One case that stuck with me was a 22-year-old barista who had missed two court dates for a speeding ticket because she couldn’t afford to take time off her zero-hours job to attend. Instead of issuing a warrant for her arrest, the lead magistrate (a 35-year-old former youth club manager) rearranged her hearing for a Saturday, waived the late fee, and set up a payment plan for the speeding fine that aligned with her irregular pay schedule. It was a small, common-sense adjustment that would have been unheard of under the old system, and it kept a young woman with no prior record from falling into a spiral of court debt and missed work.

Critics of the overhaul argue that ditching traditional wigs and formal courtroom rituals erodes the authority of the judiciary, but that argument misses the point: justice shouldn’t be intimidating or performative. The “sleekness” of these new magistrates isn’t just about their modern dress or tablet workflows—it’s about cutting out the unnecessary red tape and pageantry that made the magistracy feel distant and unapproachable for so many people. For low-level offenses that make up 95% of criminal cases in the UK, a system that prioritizes speed, fairness, and community impact over tradition is long overdue.

P.S. If you’re interested in joining the new magistracy in your local area, the 2024 national recruitment window opens on 15 May. You don’t need a law degree or formal judicial experience to apply—you just need to be over 18, have lived in the UK for at least three years, and have a commitment to fair, community-centered justice. All new magistrates receive 12 weeks of paid training and a stipend for travel and childcare costs while serving.

I’d spent three summers avoiding Grandpa’s clock repair shop, convinced the obvious truth was all that mattered: broken timepieces were USELESS, and the man who hoarded them was just stuck in the past. When he tore his rotator cuff last spring, though, Mom insisted I help out three days a week, sorting screws and sanding clock cases while he supervised.

I grumbled through the first week, staring at shelves of dented cuckoos and tarnished pocket watches, wondering why anyone would waste money fixing something that cost less to replace. That changed when Mrs. Hale pushed through the door, her wool coat dotted with rain, clutching a beat-up 1970s cuckoo clock so chipped its painted edelweiss was barely visible.

“It won’t cuckoo anymore,” she said, her voice wobbly. “I don’t care what it costs.”

I pulled up the replacement price on my phone before she finished speaking: forty-two dollars, brand new, nicer than this one. Fixing it would require tracking down obsolete gears, hours of work, twice the cost. The obvious truth was clear: this was a waste of time.

Grandpa smiled and took the clock from her. “We’ll have it singing in a week, Mrs. Hale.”

When she left, I rounded on him. “That’s crazy. We’ll lose money on that piece of junk.”

He leaned back in his chair, his good arm folded across his chest. “The obvious truth is only the top layer, Lila. Look DEEPER.”

He walked me through taking the clock apart, his hand hovering over mine when I reached for the cuckoo mechanism. “CAREFUL,” he said. “The most important parts aren’t always bolted down.”

I pried the mechanism loose, and something crumpled fluttered into my palm: a scrap of notebook paper, yellowed at the edges, tucked into a gap in the pine frame, wrapped around a pressed daisy. The handwriting was scrawled, big and blocky, the kind a ten-year-old writes: For Mom, Happy Mother’s Day. The cuckoo sings just for you. Love, Tommy.

“Tommy died in a bike crash three months after he gave her that,” Grandpa said quietly. “She never opened it up, never knew the note was there. She just loved the cuckoo sound, because it was the last thing he gave her. Fixing clocks is ONLY ever about the time they hold, not the time they tell.”

I sat with that for a long time. For eleven years, I’d carried my own obvious truth: my dad left when I was five because he didn’t love us. He’d left a note on the counter that said I can’t do this, and that was all I’d ever let myself see.

That night, I sorted through a box of unclaimed pocket watches Grandpa had set aside decades ago, and a tarnished brass one caught my eye, engraved with a tiny L on the back. I pried the back off, and a folded slip of paper fell out, tucked under the dial: For my Lila, when you’re old enough to understand. I left to get clean, so I could come back. I messed up. I love you more than all the time in the world.

I looked up to find Grandpa leaning in the doorway. “I’ve had it since he dropped it off, three years after he left. He died in a car crash six months later, right before he was supposed to come see you. I didn’t give it to you because I knew TRUTH doesn’t yell. It waits, quiet, until you’re ready to look for it.”

I’d NEVER cried over my dad before that night. I’d spent years hating him for abandoning us, clinging to the obvious line of his note, never bothering to look for the rest of the story.

A week later, Javi, a nineteen-year-old with a tattoo of a guitar on his wrist, came in with a dented pocket watch his dad had left him when he died of a heart attack two months prior. I didn’t check the replacement price first. I didn’t roll my eyes at the chipped case. I took it apart slowly, carefully, and found an engraving tucked under the mainspring, so small I needed a magnifying glass to read it: First day sober, 10/12/2019. For my boy, the reason I tried.

When I handed Javi the ticking watch, he held it to his chest and cried. He told me he’d spent his whole life thinking his dad only cared about drinking, that the only memories he had were of missed birthdays and empty beer cans. “It feels like we’re finally TOGETHER again,” he said.

I used to think WORTH was printed on price tags, that truth was the first thing you saw when you looked at something, or someone. Now I know MOST of the truths that matter are tucked into gaps, hidden under dials, behind cuckoo mechanisms, in the spaces no one bothers to check.

The world is full of loud, obvious truths: broken things are garbage, people leave because they don’t care, love is something you say out loud. But the REAL truths, the ones that stitch your heart back together, that change how you see every part of your life? They never shout. They wait, quiet, for anyone brave enough to look past the surface.

But to judge this program by 2024 engine metrics is to miss the entire point of its existence. Before 1956, chess was widely framed as a uniquely human cognitive achievement, a marker of intelligence no machine could ever replicate; Alan Turing had drafted a theoretical chess algorithm a decade earlier, but it had never been successfully run on real, physical hardware. For chess nerds and tech historians alike, IBM’s 1956 chess program is less a playable game and more a foundational artifact: clunky, slow, and laughably bad at chess by modern standards, but endlessly impressive for doing something no machine had ever done before."

The Arctic, broadly defined as the region north of the Arctic Circle, falls under polar climate regimes shaped by extreme limitations in solar exposure across much of the annual cycle. For roughly half of each year, large swathes of the area experience polar night, a period where the sun never rises above the horizon, eliminating any diurnal warming and leading to sustained frigid conditions. Even during the summer months, when 24-hour polar day brings continuous sunlight, the low angle of the sun’s rays means most incoming solar energy reflects off the region’s pervasive sea ice and snow cover rather than warming the air and surfaces. In the warmest, southernmost coastal Arctic areas, temperatures may climb just above 10°C (50°F) for two to four weeks at the peak of summer, while interior and higher elevation sites remain well below freezing even in the heart of the warm season.

For the vast majority of Arctic land and sea areas, the stretch of time where temperatures hold well below freezing lasts between 8 and 10 months annually. Winter lows regularly drop below -40°C (-40°F) in inland, ice-covered regions, and even milder coastal zones see extended multi-month stretches of temperatures hovering between -20°C and -30°C. While small, localized microclimates at the absolute southern edge of Arctic tundra may see slightly longer periods of milder conditions, these are narrow outliers that do not shift the dominant thermal pattern across the region’s vast, largely uninhabited expanse. Climate change has brought more frequent short warm spells in recent decades, but these anomalous events still do not account for a significant portion of the annual calendar across most of the Arctic.

Hey everyone, let’s kick this off with a super relatable question: how many of you have chugged a gas station coffee before an 8am exam, or cracked an energy drink to pull a last-minute study all-nighter? Yeah, I see almost all your hands—most of us have relied on that little caffeine pick-me-up at some point, right? Today we’re breaking down just how powerful that common compound is, by walking through what would happen if you gulped down 100 grams of pure, concentrated caffeine powder—something that’s sold online as a workout or study supplement sometimes, so this is actually important info to have.

First, let’s anchor everything to a regular dose of caffeine most of us consume without a second thought. A standard 12oz coffee has about 120 milligrams of caffeine, so that’s a dose that’s totally safe for almost all healthy teens and adults, giving you that gentle focus and energy bump without any major side effects.

Now, a dose of caffeine that starts to cause really uncomfortable, disruptive symptoms is around 1 gram—so that’s 1000 milligrams, or 8 full cups of coffee chugged all at once. At that dose, you’d almost certainly feel jittery enough that you can’t sit still, have a pounding, racing heart, feel panicky for no reason, and your stomach would twist up so bad you’d probably throw up. That’s your body’s built-in safety mechanism, trying to dump the excess caffeine before it can do more harm.

Next, let’s talk about the dose of caffeine that’s linked to severe, life-threatening harm for most people. For a 150-pound teen or adult, that dose lands somewhere between 10 and 15 grams, depending on your body size, any pre-existing heart conditions, and even if you’re on other meds that interact with caffeine. I know that sounds abstract, so let’s put it in coffee terms: that’s 80 to 120 full cups of coffee all at once. That’s physically impossible to drink without throwing up long before you hit that amount—unless you’re dealing with pure, concentrated caffeine powder, which packs that entire dangerous dose into a tiny amount that fits in a single teaspoon. Wild, right?

Now let’s get to the 100 gram amount we’re talking about today. That’s 10 times the minimum dose that causes severe, life-threatening harm for almost everyone, even people who drink caffeine every single day and have built up a small tolerance. Pure caffeine absorbs super fast into your bloodstream, too—so your body wouldn’t have time to trigger vomiting to get rid of it before most of that dose hits your system.

Within 15 to 30 minutes, that massive dose would overstimulate your central nervous system so hard that your heart would beat erratically, your blood pressure would spike to dangerous levels, you’d have seizures, and your body wouldn’t be able to regulate your breathing or heart function anymore. Even if you got emergency medical care immediately, that amount of caffeine is so far beyond what our bodies are built to process that you’d almost certainly suffer permanent, catastrophic damage to your brain and vital organs.

The big takeaway here is that caffeine is a drug, just like any other, and the difference between a harmless dose and a catastrophic one is tiny when you’re working with pure, powdered versions, not the diluted stuff in coffee or soda. That’s why the FDA has warned people against using bulk pure caffeine supplements—most of us don’t have a scale at home precise enough to measure milligrams, so it’s way too easy to accidentally take a dose that can upend your life forever.

# Stop Chasing 8 Hours: The Science-Backed Sleep Routine That Actually Works
Posted on October 12, 2024 by Maeve Carter | Sleep & Wellness

It’s 2:47 AM, and you’re staring at the crack of light under your bedroom door, replaying the offhand comment your coworker made at 3 PM, the unopened electric bill on your counter, and that one time in 2017 you tripped over a curb in front of your crush. Your phone glows 12 inches from your face, algorithm serving up a steady stream of cat rescue videos and “5 AM morning routine” reels that feel more like a personal attack than advice. If this sounds familiar, you’re not alone: the CDC reports 1 in 3 U.S. adults fail to get consistent, restful sleep, and most of us are blaming the wrong thing: that we’re not hitting that magical 8-hour mark.

Here’s the secret no melatonin gummy brand wants you to know: Sleep quality matters far more than quantity. Sleep unfolds in 90-minute cycles, moving from light doze to deep restorative sleep (the phase that repairs your cells and regulates your mood) to REM, the dream state that supports memory and cognitive function. If you wake up mid-cycle (even after 8 full hours), you’ll feel groggy, irritable, and like you barely slept. But wake up at the end of a cycle, after 7.5 or 9 hours, and you’ll be alert before your alarm even goes off. I learned this the hard way, after 6 months of chugging 10mg melatonin gummies, setting 7 staggered alarms, and still dragging through my workdays. It took ditching generic “no screens before bed” advice for a structured, science-backed routine to turn me from a night-owl insomniac to someone who actually looks forward to bedtime.

First, build a non-negotiable 90-minute wind-down buffer. That’s right, not 30 minutes, not an hour: 90. Your prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain that handles work, stress, and decision-making, needs that much time to shift out of “goal mode” into rest. This means no work emails, no intense Netflix dramas, and no scrolling TikTok or Instagram (even with blue light filters—studies show the cognitive stimulation of scrolling is just as disruptive to sleep as blue light itself). Instead, fill this time with low-stakes, tactile activities: fold the laundry you’ve been ignoring, wash dishes by hand, color in a cheap kids’ coloring book, or knit a lopsided scarf. Halfway through this buffer, do a 2-minute brain dump: grab a physical notebook (not your notes app) and jot down every nagging to-do, lingering worry, or random idea, with a quick note of when you’ll handle it (e.g., “Fix client typo 9 AM tomorrow”). This tells your brain it doesn’t need to hold onto those thoughts overnight—they’re safe, and you’ll deal with them later. Finally, drop your thermostat to 60-67°F: the National Sleep Foundation found this range is optimal for sleep, as your body needs to drop its core temperature by 1-2 degrees to fall and stay asleep. I used to keep my apartment at a balmy 72°F to save on heating bills; switching to 65°F cut the time it took me to fall asleep by 20 minutes almost immediately.

Second, stop self-medicating with over-the-counter sleep aids. Most melatonin gummies on the market contain 10-20mg of the hormone, 5-10x the 1-2mg dose recommended for occasional sleeplessness. Excess melatonin disrupts your body’s natural production of the hormone, leading to next-day grogginess, brain fog, and even worse long-term sleep issues. Save melatonin for jet lag, not nightly use. If you want a natural boost, try a 4-oz glass of tart cherry juice (it contains small, natural amounts of melatonin and tryptophan) or a cup of chamomile tea an hour before bed. And don’t forget about caffeine’s sneaky half-life: caffeine stays in your system for 6-8 hours, so that 3 PM iced latte you drink to power through the afternoon slump? It’s still 50% active in your body at 9 PM, cutting your deep sleep by up to 20% even if you fall asleep easily.

Third, follow the 20-minute rule religiously. If you’re lying in bed and can’t fall asleep after 20 minutes (no clock-watching—just estimate), get out of bed. Don’t lie there stressing about how little sleep you’re going to get, and don’t reach for your phone. Your brain needs to associate your bed with only two things: sleep and intimacy. If you lie awake stressing or scrolling, your brain starts to see bed as a place for anxiety and stimulation, not rest. Instead, go sit in a dimly lit corner of your home, read a physical book (nothing too thrilling—poetry, old memoirs, or that textbook you never finished for college work great), and only go back to bed when you feel heavy-eyed. I used to lie awake for 2+ hours stressing about sleep; now, I’m usually back in bed and asleep within 15 minutes of getting up.

This routine isn’t about being perfect. Some nights, you’ll stay up late binging a show, have a glass of wine with dinner, or lie awake replaying an awkward moment. That’s normal. But when you make these small, consistent changes—prioritizing cycles over 8 hours, building a real wind-down routine, ditching excess melatonin—you’ll notice a difference in days. A quick note: If you’re consistently struggling to sleep for weeks on end, talk to a doctor—chronic insomnia can be a sign of underlying mental or physical health issues, and this routine isn’t a replacement for professional care. This week, try adding just one part of this routine to your schedule: start with the 2-minute brain dump, or drop your thermostat by 5 degrees. Let me know in the comments what your go-to sleep hack is—sweet dreams!

RTE’s humming, my heart’s still running…
Back to you.

# Proposal for New Cross-Listed Undergraduate Course: HIST 375 / ANTH 342 / ANSC 315: The History of the World, as Told by Dogs
Submitted by the Department of History, College of Arts and Sciences  
To the University Curriculum Committee  
Date: October 12, 2024  
Requested Implementation: 2025–2026 Academic Year

---

## 1. Course Overview
| Detail | Specification |
|--------|---------------|
| Credits | 3 (2 75-minute lectures + 1 50-minute discussion section weekly) |
| Prerequisites | One 100-level course in History, Anthropology, or Animal Science, or instructor permission |
| Enrollment Cap | 45 (to facilitate small-group discussion and primary source analysis) |
| General Education Alignment | Fulfills requirements for Critical Analysis of Human Society and Global Diversity |

---

## 2. Course Rationale
Traditional world history curricula are overwhelmingly anthropocentric, framing non-human animals as passive background features or disposable resources rather than dynamic actors shaping the trajectory of human societies. Dogs are uniquely positioned to disrupt this bias: as the first domesticated species, with 20,000+ years of co-evolutionary history with humans, they have been present at every major global turning point, from the settlement of the Americas to the expansion of European colonialism to the 20th century struggle for disability justice.

For too long, popular and scholarly narratives have reduced dogs to loyal, uncomplicated companions, erasing how their predatory evolutionary heritage as wild wolves shaped their value to human communities, from hunting large Pleistocene game to enforcing racialized state control. Centering dogs as historical narrators allows students to interrogate core themes of world history—settlement, hierarchy, violence, exchange, and identity—from a radically new perspective, while engaging with cutting-edge scholarship in animal studies, decolonial history, and environmental humanities. This course fills a critical gap in the university’s curriculum, which currently offers no 300-level courses centered on non-human animal history.

---

## 3. Course Description
This course traces 20,000 years of global history through the lived experiences of dogs, moving beyond anthropocentric narratives of “human progress” to examine how dogs have shaped, and been shaped by, shifts in human subsistence, governance, warfare, and culture.

We begin with the contested domestication of wolves in Eurasia, evaluating how early human communities leveraged dogs’ predatory instincts to hunt large game, defend settlements, and facilitate the long-distance settlement of the Americas and Oceania. We then explore pre-modern societies, analyzing how dogs served as symbols of royal power, religious ritual, and class status across medieval Europe, the Islamic Golden Age, and pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. A core 4-week unit examines the role of dogs in European imperial expansion, analyzing how colonial administrators selectively bred dogs for heightened predatory aggression to police enslaved populations, suppress Indigenous resistance, and enforce racial hierarchies across the Global South. The course concludes with an examination of 20th and 21st century dog history, including their roles in global warfare, disability justice, civil rights organizing, and digital media culture.

Throughout the semester, students will engage with diverse primary sources—archeological remains, medieval hunt manuals, colonial administrative records, military reports, memoirs, social media content, and oral histories—to center dogs as active historical agents rather than passive accessories to human life.

---

## 4. Student Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Critique anthropocentric frameworks of world history by centering non-human animal actors as drivers of historical change;
2. Evaluate how the predatory evolutionary origins of *Canis lupus familiaris* have shaped dogs’ functional and symbolic roles across diverse global societies, from Pleistocene hunting partnerships to 21st century working K9 programs;
3. Analyze diverse primary and secondary sources to construct evidence-based arguments about historical change, adhering to disciplinary standards for historical and anthropological scholarship;
4. Assess the ongoing legacy of colonial dog breeding and deployment as a tool of racial capitalism and state violence, building competency in decolonial historical analysis;
5. Develop an original research project that uses dog-centered analysis to explore a global historical theme, presented in a format accessible to both academic and public audiences.

---

## 5. Sample 15-Week Syllabus
| Week | Theme | Core Readings & Activities |
|------|-------|-----------------------------|
| 1 | Introduction: Why Dog History? | Excerpts from Donna Haraway’s *The Companion Species Manifesto*; discussion of anthropocentrism in standard world history textbooks |
| 2 | Co-Evolution: The Domestication of Wolves, 20,000 BCE | Darcy Morey’s *The Dawn of the Dog* (Ch. 1–2); debate: Did wolves self-domesticate as scavengers, or did humans recruit them for their predatory hunting skill? |
| 3 | Pleistocene Partners: Dogs and the Settlement of the Globe | Archeological reports of dog burial sites in Beringia and Monte Verde, Chile; analysis of canine DNA as historical evidence |
| 4 | Dogs of Power: Medieval Aristocratic Hunting | Excerpts from 14th-century English hunt manuals; discussion of how selective breeding for specialized predatory traits reinforced feudal class hierarchies |
| 5 | Dogs Across the Pre-Modern Global South | Fadwa El Guindi’s “Salukis in Bedouin Society”; analysis of pre-Columbian Mesoamerican dog ritual and food systems |
| 6 | Midterm Review | Guided study session; peer review of primary source analysis outlines |
| 7 | Midterm Exam + Break | In-class essay exam covering Weeks 1–6 |
| 8 | Colonial Canines: Predatory Tools of Imperial Violence | 1896 British Colonial Police Dog Breeding Manual (primary source); Reuben Ben-Ahron’s “Dogs as Weapons of Colonial Control in South Africa” |
| 9 | Slaver Hounds and Racial Capitalism in the Americas | Christopher Schmidt’s “Slave Patrol Dogs and the Origins of American Policing”; oral histories of enslaved people’s encounters with hunting dogs |
| 10 | Dogs of World War I and II | Excerpts from Maria Goodavage’s *Soldier Dogs*; guest lecture from a local U.S. Army K9 handler (virtual attendance option for students with dog allergies/fear) |
| 11 | Civil Rights Canines: Oppression and Solidarity | Michael V. Gomez’s “Bull Connor’s Dogs and the Visual Politics of Civil Rights”; oral histories of service dogs for Black disabled veterans |
| 12 | Disability Justice: Service Dogs and Access Rights, 1970–Present | Mia Carter’s “Service Dogs and the Politics of Access”; analysis of ADA testimony as primary source |
| 13 | Digital Dogs: Influencers and Global Pet Capitalism | Brooke Erin Duffy’s “Dog Influencers and the Branding of Companionhood”; analysis of TikTok dog accounts as historical artifacts |
| 14 | Final Project Workshop | Peer review of research drafts and creative project outlines |
| 15 | Final Project Presentations | 10-minute student presentations of research papers, digital exhibits, or dog biography podcasts |

---

## 6. Assessment Methods
Assessments are designed to support diverse learning styles and align with core course learning outcomes:
1. **Primary Source Analysis (20%, Due Week 8):** 1,500-word analysis of the 1896 British Colonial Police Dog Breeding Manual, evaluating how the manual’s emphasis on breeding for predatory aggression was tied to colonial efforts to suppress anti-imperial organizing in South Africa.
2. **Midterm Examination (25%):** In-class exam with two essay questions assessing student understanding of domestication, pre-modern dog history, and core theoretical frameworks of animal studies.
3. **Final Research Project (40%):** Students choose one of three formats: (a) 2,500-word academic research paper; (b) digital exhibit (using Omeka) showcasing dog-centered primary sources; or (c) 10-minute “dog biography” podcast tracing the life of a specific historical dog as a lens for global change. All projects must engage with at least three primary sources and course themes of non-human agency and structural inequality.
4. **Weekly Participation (15%):** Evaluated based on in-class discussion contributions, 200-word weekly response posts, and peer feedback during the final project workshop.

---

## 7. Accessibility and Inclusivity
- This course adheres to all university accessibility policies, with accessible course materials and reasonable accommodations for students with documented disabilities.
- All optional in-person activities featuring live dogs are held in a separate, well-ventilated space with full virtual attendance options for students with dog allergies or cynophobia. Service dogs are always welcome in all course spaces per university policy.
- The syllabus includes content warnings for units covering colonial violence, enslavement, and animal cruelty, with alternative readings available for students who require them.
- Core readings prioritize scholarship from BIPOC, disabled, and Indigenous scholars to center marginalized perspectives on human-dog relationships, pushing back against the Eurocentric framing of most existing animal studies scholarship.

---

## 8. Resource Requirements
- No required hardcopy textbooks: all core readings are available as e-books through the university library to reduce student costs.
- Access to university digital archive subscriptions, including JSTOR, Project MUSE, and the British Colonial Archives digital collection.
- A $500 program budget is requested to support a guest lecture from Dr. Philip Howell, a leading scholar of colonial animal history, and to cover materials for digital exhibit projects.
- The course will be taught by Dr. Elena Marquez (Department of History), whose research focuses on decolonial animal studies and global imperial history. Dr. Marquez has six years of undergraduate teaching experience and has published three peer-reviewed articles on dog history in colonial contexts.

---

## 9. Conclusion
*The History of the World, as Told by Dogs* is a rigorous, cross-disciplinary course that pushes students to reimagine what counts as history and who (or what) counts as a historical agent. Unlike superficial popular narratives of dog companionship, this course centers the often-violent structural forces that have shaped human-dog relationships, from the leveraging of wolves’ predatory hunting skills to build settled agricultural societies to the deployment of selectively bred dogs as predatory tools of colonial and state oppression. By centering dogs as narrators, the course invites students to engage with urgent conversations about racial justice, disability rights, and human responsibility to the non-human world. We request full approval of this course for inclusion in the 2025–2026 undergraduate catalog.

| 15 | Final Project Presentations | 10-minute student presentations of research papers, digital exhibits, or dog biography podcasts |

## 6. Assessment Methods
Assessments are designed to support diverse learning styles and align with core course learning outcomes:
1. **Primary Source Analysis (20%, Due Week 8):** 1,500-word analysis of the 1896 British Colonial Police Dog Breeding Manual, evaluating how the manual’s emphasis on breeding for predatory aggression was tied to colonial efforts to suppress anti-imperial organizing in South Africa.
2. **Midterm Examination (25%):** In-class exam with two essay questions assessing student understanding of domestication, pre-modern dog history, and core theoretical frameworks of animal studies.
3. **Final Research Project (40%):** Students choose one of three formats: (a) 2,500-word academic research paper; (b) digital exhibit (using Omeka) showcasing dog-centered primary sources; or (c) 10-minute “dog biography” podcast tracing the life of a specific historical dog as a lens for global change. All projects must engage with at least three primary sources and course themes of non-human agency and structural inequality.
4. **Weekly Participation (15%):** Evaluated based on in-class discussion contributions, 200-word weekly response posts, and peer feedback during the final project workshop.

---

## 7. Accessibility and Inclusivity
- This course adheres to all university accessibility policies, with accessible course materials and reasonable accommodations for students with documented disabilities.
- All optional in-person activities featuring live dogs are held in a separate, well-ventilated space with full virtual attendance options for students with dog allergies or cynophobia. Service dogs are always welcome in all course spaces per university policy.
- The syllabus includes content warnings for units covering colonial violence, enslavement, and animal cruelty, with alternative readings available for students who require them.
- Core readings prioritize scholarship from BIPOC, disabled, and Indigenous scholars to center marginalized perspectives on human-dog relationships, pushing back against the Eurocentric framing of most existing animal studies scholarship.

---

## 8. Resource Requirements
- No required hardcopy textbooks: all core readings are available as e-books through the university library to reduce student costs.
- Access to university digital archive subscriptions, including JSTOR, Project MUSE, and the British Colonial Archives digital collection.
- A $500 program budget is requested to support a guest lecture from Dr. Philip Howell, a leading scholar of colonial animal history, and to cover materials for digital exhibit projects.
- The course will be taught by Dr. Elena Marquez (Department of History), whose research focuses on decolonial animal studies and global imperial history. Dr. Marquez has six years of undergraduate teaching experience and has published three peer-reviewed articles on dog history in colonial contexts.

---

## 9. Conclusion
*The History of the World, as Told by Dogs* is a rigorous, cross-disciplinary course that pushes students to reimagine what counts as history and who (or what) counts as a historical agent. Unlike superficial popular narratives of dog companionship, this course centers the often-violent structural forces that have shaped human-dog relationships, from the leveraging of wolves’ predatory hunting skills to build settled agricultural societies to the deployment of selectively bred dogs as predatory tools of colonial and state oppression. By centering dogs as narrators, the course invites students to engage with urgent conversations about racial justice, disability rights, and human responsibility to the non-human world. We request full approval of this course for inclusion in the 2025–2026 undergraduate catalog.
