SECTION 1
Harry Kowalski, 29, freelance graphic designer and professional avoider of phone calls from his mom, named his terrier mix Garlic Bread for extremely logical reasons: the rescue called to confirm his adoption approval exactly 0.2 seconds after he bit into a frozen garlic bread he’d microwaved 90 seconds too long, burning the roof of his mouth so bad he couldn’t say any other name for three days. The dog’s quirk, besides farting loud enough to set off the smoke alarm every time Harry plays Taylor Swift’s *Midnights*, was stealing rubber stamps. Harry sold custom stamps on Etsy for side cash, and after he left a “World’s Okayest Plant Parent” prototype on the coffee table once, Garlic Bread turned stamp hoarding into a full-time career. The trouble started when Harry, best man for his little sister Lila’s wedding the next day, set down the custom favor stamp he’d spent three hours designing—“Lila & Jake Forever, 10/14/24”, with a tiny doodle of their one-eyed rescue cat—down to answer a work email. He turned around 90 seconds later and it was gone. Garlic Bread was curled on the rug, blue ink smudged on his left ear, looking so proud he could’ve burst. Harry tried bribing him with a piece of actual garlic bread, but the dog just snuffled and trotted away, like he was holding the stamp hostage for a better ransom (probably a whole jar of peanut butter).

SECTION 2
Harry tore his 500-square-foot studio apart like a cop executing a search warrant for a very small, very specific piece of rubber. First, he dug through the couch cushions, the site of 70% of Garlic Bread’s stashes: he found 19 stamps (highlights included a very explicit bachelorette party stamp he’d forgotten he made, a possum holding a taco, and one that just said “I <3 PICKLES” in curly font) but no wedding stamp. Next, he checked the empty Cheerios box in the recycling bin, where Garlic Bread had hidden his Christmas stocking the year prior: only a corgi wearing a cowboy hat stamp, which was very cool but not helpful. He was 12 missed texts deep from Lila, who was threatening to make him do the chicken dance solo at the reception if he messed up the favors, when he remembered he’d caught Garlic Bread unrolling guest toilet paper rolls last week to shove random objects in their cardboard cores. He dumped all 8 rolls from under the sink onto the bathroom floor, unspooling each like he was wrapping a giant mummy, and found the stamp in the fourth roll, linty but perfectly intact. He whooped so loud his upstairs neighbor banged on the ceiling. That’s when Garlic Bread launched off the toilet seat, snatched the stamp right out of his hand, and bolted out the front door Harry had propped open to let in fall air. Harry sprinted after him barefoot, his ratty Baby Yoda pajama pants slipping down his hips, yelling “GARLIC BREAD I SWEAR I WILL FEED YOU ONLY BROCCOLI FOR A WEEK” while the old lady from 2B leaned out her window and cheered like it was an Olympic marathon.

SECTION 3
Harry chased Garlic Bread three blocks: past the bodega where the owner yelled “GO GET HIM, KOWALSKI!”, past the library where the librarian shushed him even as he sprinted past, all the way to the dog park he’d avoided for six months because he had a huge, stupid crush on Mia, the regular with the corgi named Muffin who brought homemade peanut butter treats. Garlic Bread skidded to a stop right at Mia’s feet, dropped the wet, lint-covered wedding stamp at her sneakers, then flopped onto his back for a belly rub. Logline: A grieving teen janitor at a Detroit community boxing gym discovers he has a rare dream-linked superpower that lets him channel the strength of his dream fights into his waking body—then risks permanent death in a brutal underground dream combat circuit to wake his narcoleptic little sister trapped in a dream coma.

### Act 1
Nineteen-year-old Javi Mendez has spent his whole life fighting just to get by: he dropped out of high school to work two jobs (gym janitor by day, late-night food delivery driver) to care for his 12-year-old sister Lila, his only family, who lives with severe narcolepsy with cataplexy. The siblings are scraping to afford a clinical trial that could ease Lila’s symptoms—until a narcoleptic episode mid-crosswalk leaves Lila trapped in a persistent vegetative state, her brain spiking with unprecedented dream activity that doctors can’t explain.
Grief-stricken, Javi falls asleep on the hospital couch wearing his late father’s tattered, too-big pro boxing gloves, and wakes up in Slumberland: a grimy, neon-drenched district of the collective unconscious, populated by dream echoes, lost souls trapped in comas, and fighters competing in the Gauntlet of Echoes, a no-holds-barred fist-fighting circuit. His old gym mentor Mister Ray—who died of a heart attack when Javi was 12, and now works as a Gauntlet trainer—greets him, explaining Javi has a rare superpower: Oneiron Fists.
The power has two non-negotiable rules: 1) Every punch landed, every bruise taken, every hour of boxing training Javi does in Slumberland translates 1:1 to his waking body. 2) If he is knocked out cold in a Gauntlet fight, he wakes with permanent amnesia of everyone he loves; if he is killed, he dies in real life from a brain aneurysm. The only way to wake Lila is to win five consecutive Gauntlet fights, earn five Wake Tokens, and trade them to the Gauntlet’s Gatekeeper to pull her soul back to the waking world.

### Act 2
Javi’s first four fights pit him against dream echoes tied to his deepest traumas, forcing him to master both his boxing skill and his superpower:
1. A 10-foot-tall echo of the drug dealer who sold his father laced painkillers that ended his pro boxing career, wielding brass knuckles made of rusted syringe needles. Javi wins with the stiff jab Mister Ray drilled into him as a kid, waking to find he can lift a 200lb heavy bag over his head with one arm.
2. An echo of the high school teacher who told Javi he’d “never be anything more than a janitor,” fighting with a whip made of failed report cards. Javi uses the footwork he honed delivering packages in Detroit snow to outmaneuver him, waking with the stamina to run 10 miles without breaking a sweat.

But the superpower has a hidden cost: every fight fueled by rage erases a small memory of Lila. After his third win, Javi can’t remember Lila’s favorite snack (cheese puffs with hot sauce); after his fourth, he forgets her birthday. His childhood best friend Mia, a pre-med student, confronts him, convinced his exhaustion and memory lapses are a breakdown—until she finds Lila’s hidden dream journal, filled with drawings of the Slumberland arena and Javi boxing in glowing blue gloves. Mia realizes Javi’s dreams are real: Lila’s trapped consciousness is watching him fight.
Javi’s final qualifying fight pits him against the Gauntlet’s undefeated reigning champion: a masked brute with Oneiron Fists of his own. Mid-fight, the champion’s mask shatters, revealing Javi’s father Mace—who didn’t abandon the family 9 years prior, but was trapped in Slumberland after fighting the Gauntlet to pay for baby Lila’s first narcolepsy treatments. The Gauntlet’s shadowy ruler, the Dream Broker, erased Mace’s memory of his family and turned him into his enforcer. Mace beats Javi within an inch of his life; Javi wakes with three broken ribs, ready to give up—until Mia reads him a note from Lila’s journal: “My brother can fight any monster, even the ones in dreams.”

### Act 3
Javi trains in both the waking world (Mia runs drills with him at the gym) and Slumberland (Mister Ray teaches him to channel love instead of rage to fuel his Oneiron Fists, turning their usual red glow a soft, bright blue). He challenges Mace to a rematch, but the Dream Broker intervenes mid-fight, revealing his endgame: he trapped Lila to lure both Javi and Mace to the Gauntlet, because a fight to the death between two blood-related Oneiron Fists users will generate enough pain energy to let him cross into the waking world and enslave every human’s dreams.
The final fight is a three-way brawl: Javi refuses to hurt Mace, instead landing precise, non-lethal punches that trigger Mace’s lost memories: a childhood lesson on how to wrap a wrist, a burnt-toast breakfast the day before he fell into his coma, the sound of baby Lila’s laugh. When Mace’s memory returns, the two team up against the Dream Broker, a 20-foot shadow monster made of broken dream fragments and the pain of thousands of trapped coma patients.
Javi realizes his Oneiron Fists have a unique, unrecorded ability: he can channel the strength of every lost soul trapped in Slumberland. All across the arena, the hands of coma patients and forgotten dreamers glow blue, their power flowing into Javi’s fists. Javi and Mace land a simultaneous double uppercut, shattering the Dream Broker into a million tiny dream particles.
Javi trades his five Wake Tokens plus Mace’s champion token to the Gatekeeper. Back in the waking world, Lila wakes up minutes later, holding a drawing of Javi and Mace boxing together. Mace, who had been in an unmarked coma in a nearby hospital for 9 years, wakes up hours later, his old boxing gloves in his lap.

### Resolution
Six months later, Javi, Mace, and Lila run free boxing clinics for at-risk kids at the Eastside Gym. Javi still uses his Oneiron Fists—mostly to lift Lila onto his shoulders to reach the top shelf of snack cabinets, and to knock out would-be robbers when he’s on delivery runs. The mid-credits scene shows a dozen people across the globe waking up from comas, their fists glowing soft blue, as Mister Ray watches from Slumberland, grinning.

subject: application for junior circular economy strategist role

dear jade marlow, lead of circular strategy at jupiter waste solutions,

i’m writing to apply for the junior circular economy strategist role posted on the industry job board last week, and i want to lead with something most applicants would jettison from their opening line: i know jupiter has a pretty bad reputation right now. i’ve read the jabs from local journalists about the 2023 unauthorized dumping scandal, the rulings from state environmental judges about misreported residential waste diversion rates, and the snide comments from peers at industry conferences that frame your team as a case study in what not to do for green compliance. most candidates would write off applying here entirely, but that juncture of public distrust and urgent pressure to improve is exactly why this role feels like such a perfect fit.

for the last three years, i’ve worked as a waste diversion coordinator for a small regional non-profit that serves three rural counties, where my core job was to untangle the jumbled mess of data tracking, cross-jurisdiction regulatory rules, and misaligned staff training that left the organization at risk of losing $2.1m in annual state funding. i learned to juggle weekly audits of 12 drop-off centers, translate dense circular economy jargon for part-time frontline staff with no formal sustainability training, and overhaul our public reporting process to cut error rates from 32% to less than 2% in 18 months. i’m not jaded by messy, high-stakes turnaround work—if anything, i seek it out, because it’s the only work that feels like it makes a tangible difference, rather than just repeating empty talking points for press releases.

to be clear: i’m not here to jest about easy fixes or pretend that rebuilding trust will be fast. i’ve reviewed the full 2024 consent decree your team signed with the department of environmental quality, and the requirement to hit 75% diversion by 2027 isn’t just a marketing goal—it’s a legally binding mandate that will require overhauling almost every core process your team currently uses. i also saw that you just brought on a new head of operations who led the 2021 zero-waste rollout for the regional grocery cooperative, which tells me your leadership isn’t just paying lip service to fixing past mistakes.

as for my credentials: i hold a master’s in industrial circular economy, my senior thesis on low-cost construction waste sorting methods was published in the journal of sustainable waste management last june, and i’ve consulted for four small waste haulers on fixing their reporting systems to avoid regulatory fines. but the weird, relevant detail i want to lead with here is that i collect vintage waste management souvenir pins, and the oldest pin in my collection is a chipped 1987 jupiter waste “we keep jacksonville clean” pin i found at a flea market two years ago. it’s sat on my desk ever since, a tiny, jolting reminder that even companies with messy, fraught pasts were once built on a promise to serve their local communities, not just cut corners to hit quarterly targets.

i know right now, jupiter’s reputation is a joke in most industry circles, and rebuilding that will require more than just fancy ad campaigns or new jargon to fudge data. it will require someone who’s comfortable digging into jumbled spreadsheets, talking through concerns with frustrated local residents, and juggling regulatory requirements while finding low-cost, practical fixes that actually work. i’d jump at the chance to bring that experience to your team, and to help turn jupiter from a cautionary tale into a leader in transparent, community-focused waste management.

i’ve attached my resume, my full thesis, and a one-page outline of three low-lift changes your team could implement in the next 90 days to boost diversion rates by 8% without additional operating budget. i’d be thrilled to chat at your convenience, even if it’s just to bounce ideas around about how to move past the missteps of the last few years.

sincerely,
jamie rivera
(555) 123-4567 | jamie.rivera.waste@gmail.com | linkedin.com/in/jamieriveracirculareconomy

Folks, let me tell you about the quiet worker that runs every damn thing we hold dear—the rise of sourdough in a bakery oven on Main Street, the weld holding a bridge over the Ohio, the first crumpled dollar tucked into a teen’s lemonade stand cash box. It’s got a fancy name, Gibbs free energy, but don’t let the lab coat lingo fool you: this is the decider, the unforgiving, fair judge of what sticks and what fades to smoke. It don’t care about press releases or campaign promises, don’t care if you call yourself a Democrat or a Republican. It only cares what you build, and whether that build’s got the guts to outlast the mess of the world.


It breaks down real simple, if you let it: take the sweat you pour in, the heat of your effort, the cash you sink into a dream, the hours you stay up sanding a floor or writing a lesson plan—that’s the first part, the grit you bring to the table, the raw energy you put into any job. Subtract the chaos you can’t outrun: the supply chain snags, the rain that washes out the county fair, the red tape that makes a small business owner wait six months for a permit. Multiply that mess by the temperature of the times, the urgency of the moment, the hunger of a community for something better. If what’s left is less than zero? That thing’s gonna grow, gonna move, gonna last, no one having to stand over it with a whip. If it’s more? You can holler all you want, throw a million dollars at it, it’s gonna crumble, same as a house built on sand.


That’s why we don’t fight the rule—we work with it. When we send tax cuts to small businesses instead of billionaire CEOs, we’re pouring good, honest grit into the system, upping the effort that goes straight to the communities that need it most. When we cut the unnecessary red tape that keeps rural hospitals from opening, keeps solar farms from powering small towns, keeps student debt borrowers from getting the relief they earned? We’re cutting the chaos, the dead weight that drags progress down. When we meet this moment of climate crisis and middle-class decline with the urgency it deserves, we’re matching the temperature of the times to the work we’re doing. That’s how we get reactions that run on their own: union factories churning out EV batteries that don’t quit, family farms growing cover crops that feed the soil and the community, affordable housing that stays affordable for generations, no strings attached.


This ain’t just chemistry for the kids in AP class, folks. This is the rule of the road for this country we love. We don’t build progress by yelling louder or cutting corners or pretending chaos don’t exist. We build it by putting in the work, by cutting the mess that holds us back, by meeting the moment we’re given, not the moment we wish we had. Gibbs don’t play favorites, but he rewards the folks who show up, who do the math, who care more about what lasts than what makes the six o’clock news. That’s the American deal, right there: show up, put in the work, build something that outlasts you.

Today, at the 54th Annual Grammy Awards, the Recording Academy honors the talent and creativity of the artists, musicians, and producers who are the creators of the best recordings of the past year.

Staged on 12 February 2012 at the Staples Center in Los Angeles, California¹, this ceremony marks a historic juncture in the Academy’s 54-year mission to recognize excellence across 30 distinct genre fields, spanning from classical orchestral composition to progressive R&B production, from Appalachian folk storytelling to mainstream pop innovation. Eligibility for the 54th Annual Grammy Awards extended to recordings released between 1 October 2010 and 30 September 2011², a period defined by boundary-pushing cross-genre collaboration, independent artist breakthroughs, and seismic shifts in digital music distribution that redefined how global audiences engage with recorded sound.

A core tenet of this year’s proceedings, reaffirmed by Recording Academy CEO Neil Portnow in his pre-ceremony address to voting members and industry stakeholders, is *the centering of artistic integrity over commercial chart performance as the primary criterion for nomination and victory*³. Unlike peer industry awards that prioritize sales metrics, streaming volume, or social media engagement, Grammy nominations are determined via a two-tiered peer review process: first, specialized screening committees of practicing creators verify category eligibility and technical merit, then full voting members cast confidential ballots for nominees and winners across all non-specialized award fields⁴.

This year’s marquee General Field categories— the only set of awards open to all recording artists regardless of genre affiliation—reflect the unprecedented breadth of 2011’s recorded output. Nominations for *Album of the Year*, the Academy’s highest competitive honor, include: 21 by Adele, a soul-inflected pop project that spent 13 non-consecutive weeks atop the Billboard 200 chart; Wasting Light by Foo Fighters, recorded entirely on analog tape in frontman Dave Grohl’s home garage to reject overproduced digital studio norms; *Born This Way* by Lady Gaga, a dance-pop manifesto centered on LGBTQ+ advocacy and radical self-acceptance; Doo-Wops & Hooligans by Bruno Mars, a retro-inflected debut that revived 1960s soul and doo-wop sensibilities for 21st-century audiences; and Loud by Rihanna, a dancehall and EDM-influenced pop record that spawned seven top-10 Billboard Hot 100 singles⁵. Notably, *Adele’s 21 is the only 21st-century Album of the Year nominee to be certified diamond by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) prior to the awards ceremony*, a rare milestone that reflects both critical acclaim and mass cultural resonance.

Beyond the General Field, the 54th Grammy Awards introduces three new competitive categories to recognize emerging and underrecognized creative practices: Best Dance/Electronic Album, Best Classical Compendium, and Best Country Duo/Group Performance⁶. This expansion reflects the Academy’s ongoing commitment to *evolving its categorical framework to center marginalized creators and emerging production techniques*, responding to 12 years of feedback from dance music creators who previously competed in broader, mismatched categories (e.g., Best Pop Instrumental Performance) with little parity for electronic-specific production craft.

A solemn, unifying undercurrent anchors this year’s live telecast, following the unexpected passing of iconic pop vocalist Whitney Houston on 11 February 2012, less than 24 hours before the ceremony’s live broadcast⁷. The Academy adjusted its pre-planned program overnight to include a tribute performance led by Jennifer Hudson, who will perform Houston’s 1992 landmark cover of *I Will Always Love You*—a recording that won the 36th Annual Grammy Award for Record of the Year in 1994, and remains one of the best-selling singles of all time⁸. This tribute underscores the Academy’s dual institutional mission to celebrate the year’s new creative contributions while honoring *the intergenerational legacy of artists who shape the very definition of recorded excellence* for decades after their work is first released.

Finally, all proceeds from the official ceremony after-party, silent auction, and VIP pre-show reception will be directed to the Recording Academy’s MusiCares Foundation⁹, a charitable organization that provides financial, medical, and housing support to music creators facing crisis, including uninsured medical costs, housing instability, and targeted mental health resources for touring and studio professionals.

---
### Formal Notations
¹ Recording Academy, *54th Annual Grammy Awards Operations Manual* (2012), p. 12. The Staples Center (rebranded Crypto.com Arena in 2021) hosted the Grammy Awards for its 12th consecutive year in 2012, with a live in-person audience of 18,000 industry professionals and guests, plus a global broadcast audience of 39 million viewers across 190 international territories.
² Recording Academy, *54th Annual Grammy Awards Eligibility Guidelines* (2011), § 2.1. Eligibility excludes recordings released exclusively for promotional use, film and television soundtracks submitted for Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences award consideration, and recordings with less than 51% original, previously unreleased content.
³ Neil Portnow, Opening Address to Recording Academy Voting Membership (8 November 2011), Recording Academy Institutional Archive, Los Angeles, CA.
⁴ Recording Academy, *Voting Procedures Handbook (2012 Revision)*, § 3.2–3.5. Specialized niche categories (e.g., Best Classical Orchestral Performance, Best Bluegrass Album) are voted on exclusively by voting members who have demonstrated professional expertise via credited work in the relevant genre field.
⁵ Recording Academy, Official 54th Annual Grammy Awards Nominations Announcement (30 November 2011). Nomination totals were led by Kanye West, who received seven nominations for his solo album *My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy* and collaborative album with Jay-Z, *Watch the Throne*.
⁶ Recording Academy, Category Expansion Announcement (15 June 2011). The addition of Best Dance/Electronic Album marked the first new category for dance music creators since the introduction of Best Dance Recording in 1998.
⁷ Associated Press, “Whitney Houston Dies at 48 in Los Angeles Hotel Room” (11 February 2012). Houston’s death occurred at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, the site of the annual Grammy pre-party hosted by Clive Davis, Houston’s long-time career mentor.
⁸ Recording Academy Awards Database, 36th Annual Grammy Awards (1994). Houston’s *I Will Always Love You* spent 14 weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100, a record for a female solo artist at the time of its release, and has sold over 24 million copies worldwide as of 2024.
⁹ MusiCares Foundation, *Annual Report 2012*, p. 47. Events associated with the 54th Grammy Awards raised $2.1 million for MusiCares, a 12% increase over funds raised during the 53rd Annual ceremony.

Write a review of "Laureates and twins" for professionals in the field of psychology without the use of commas and make sure to include the phrase "well worth watching".
Laureates and Twins delivers a nuanced empirically rigorous exploration of twin study methodology and trait heritability that is tailored to the needs of psychology professionals. The work examines rare cohorts of identical twins where one member has achieved elite research status as a Nobel laureate to unpack the complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors that shape extreme achievement outcomes. It avoids the oversimplified heritability framing that defines most mainstream content about twin research by centering extended commentary from leading behavioral geneticists and personality psychology researchers. It walks viewers through common limitations of classical twin study designs including assumptions around equal environments and range restriction that even early career psychology researchers often struggle to apply correctly. It also presents original preliminary findings from secondary analysis of international twin registry data that point to understudied non shared environmental variables that drive divergent high achievement trajectories. The content balances deep methodological context with engaging personal narrative from the twin pairs featured to keep viewers engaged without sacrificing empirical rigor. It includes supplementary discussion of how twin study frameworks can be adjusted to reduce bias in research on underrepresented populations which fills a key gap in many existing educational resources for psychology researchers. It is well worth watching for any psychology professional working in behavioral genetics developmental psychology personality science or research methods education.

# 7 Delightfully Weird Facts About the Dutch Language (No Throat-Clearing Required)

If you’ve ever lingered by an Amsterdam canal, stroopwafel in hand, and overheard a group of locals chatting, you’ve probably had the same thought I did during my first week in the Netherlands: “Wait, is that English? No, German? Wait, why does it sound like everyone is quietly clearing their throat?”
Dutch has long been the punchline of European language jokes, written off as “English with a cold” or “German-lite for people who hate case endings.” But after six months of fumbling through grocery store orders, making friends with local baristas, and failing (repeatedly) to pronounce gracht (canal) correctly, I learned Dutch is far more charming, clever, and influential than its reputation suggests. Let’s dive into the most surprising facts about this underrated West Germanic gem.

---

### It’s the uncredited parent of one of the world’s youngest official languages
Most people know Afrikaans is spoken in South Africa and Namibia, but few realize it’s a direct descendant of 17th-century Dutch, brought to the Cape by Dutch East India Company colonists. For centuries, Afrikaans was dismissed as “kitchen Dutch” — a rough, uneducated dialect of the parent language — until it was formally recognized as a separate language in 1925. Even today, the two are so mutually intelligible that a Dutch tourist can order coffee, ask for directions, and have a casual conversation with an Afrikaans speaker in Cape Town without either struggling to follow along. - गाउँमा स्थानीय थारु परिवारसँग बसेर नाश्ता गर्नुहोस्, उनीहरूको दैनिक जीवनशैली, परम्परा, वेशभूषा बारे जान्नुहोस्। थारु लोकनृत्य 'ठाकुर नृत्य' हेर्नुहोस्, सिक्न चाहनुभए सिक्न सक्नुहुन्छ।
- दिउँसो १ बजे उनीहरूको परम्परागत खाना जस्तै घोंगही, सिंघौड़ा, भात, साग खानुहोस्।
- बेलुका ३ बजे गाउँको स्वयं सहायता समूहबाट थारु लोक कलाका सामान (हातको बुनाईको टोपी, झोला, देसी घी) किन्नुहोस्। साँझ ६ बजे विराटनगर फर्की हातखोला चोकको मलाई कुल्फी खानुहोस्।

### दिन ७: धरान शहर र नमस्ते झरना यात्रा
- सुबह ७ बजे निस्कनुहोस्, विराटनगरबाट करिब १ घण्टाको सवारीमा धरान शहर पुग्न सकिन्छ। पहिलो स्थान **बुधा सुब्बा मन्दिर** जानुहोस्, यो धरानको प्रसिद्ध धार्मिक स्थल हो, मन्दिरबाट शहरको सम्पूर्ण दृश्य देख्न सकिन्छ।
- १० बजे धरान घण्टा घर, धरान पार्क घुम्नुहोस्, स्थानीय बजारमा घुमेर सामान किन्ने मन छ भने किन्नुहोस्।
- दिउँसो १ बजे धरानको प्रसिद्ध मोमो घरमा मोमो र चाउचाउ खानुहोस्, यसको स्वाद विशेष मानिन्छ।
- ३ बजे धरानबाट करिब ३० मिनेटको सवारीमा **नमस्ते झरना** जानुहोस्: १०० मिटर अग्लो यस झरनाको पानीमा खेल्न सकिन्छ, प्रकृतिको सुन्दर दृश्यको आनन्द लिनुहोस्। साँझ ७ बजे विराटनगर फर्कनुहोस्।

- दिउँसो १ बजे संस्थान नजिकैको मैथिली खाना घरमा मैथिली थाली खानुहोस्, जसमा चोखा, छोले, साग, पुठी, मासु तरकारी आदि रहेको हुन्छ।
- ३ बजे महिला स्वयं सहायता समूहको कार्यालय जानुहोस्: विराटनगरका स्थानीय महिलाहरूले बनाएको मिथिला छापका कपडा, श्रृंगार सामान, अचार, लड्डु आदि किन्नुहोस्, यसले स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रमा मद्दत हुन्छ।

- बेलुका ६ बजे सुभगा चोक र हजुरपुर चोकमा खरीददारी गर्नुहोस्: तेराईका विशेष कपडा (मिथिला छापको साडी, कुर्ता), मिठाई, अचार आदि किन्नुहोस्। राती होटल नजिकैको रेस्टुरेन्टमा मैथिली सेहत खानुहोस्।

# Tending the Knot: The Quiet Revolution of Wilderness Preservation
In late August 2019, a line of thunderstorms barreled across Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, turning the glassy surface of Lac La Croix into a churn of whitecaps. I was 22, three days into my first solo backcountry trip, and I fumbled to tie a bowline knot around the gnarled root of a 200-year-old white pine, my fingers numb with cold rain. My grandma had taught me that knot when I was 8, on a camping trip in the Superior National Forest, saying it would hold fast even when the rope was pulled tight. I remember thinking as I pulled the knot taut that day, watching the wind tear leaves from the canopy above, that I was only securing a canoe. Wilderness, I realized in that breathless moment, is not a collection of isolated trees or lakes, but a living knot of interdependence: the pine whose root held my canoe also sheltered a family of merlins, whose droppings fed the moss that anchored the shoreline, which filtered the water that fed the wild rice that had sustained Anishinaabe communities for a thousand years. To preserve wilderness is not, as early 20th-century conservationists once argued, to lock away a pristine snapshot of nature untainted by humans. It is to tend to these tangled knots of ecology, culture, and memory, ensuring they do not fray under the weight of extraction, exclusion, and climate collapse.

For much of the 20th century, wilderness preservation was rooted in a dangerous fiction: the idea that wild spaces are places untouched by human hands. The 1964 Wilderness Act, which codified federal protection for lands “untrammeled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain,” erased the 10,000-year history of Indigenous stewardship that shaped nearly every ecosystem now classified as wilderness in the United States. The Anishinaabe did not simply visit the Boundary Waters; they tended it, using prescribed burns to regenerate berry patches, harvesting wild rice in ways that replenished the beds for future harvests, and managing beaver populations to maintain wetland health. The “pristine” forest I hiked through in 2019 was not a natural accident, but the product of millennia of careful, reciprocal care. *Wilderness is not a museum of uninhabited nature, but a dynamic, interwoven tapestry stitched over millennia by human and nonhuman hands alike.* To fail to recognize this is to cut critical strands of the knot that sustains wilderness health, leaving ecosystems vulnerable to collapse when they lose the stewardship practices that shaped them. In recent years, co-management agreements between tribal nations and the U.S. Forest Service have begun to repair this damage, returning decision-making power over lands like the Boundary Waters to the communities who know them best. This is not a compromise of preservation values; it is a return to the truth of what wilderness has always been: a shared inheritance, tended collectively.

Preservation’s second, equally harmful legacy is its long association with elite recreation. Early conservation leaders like John Muir framed the wilderness as a refuge for overworked, middle-class white Americans seeking escape from industrial cities, a framing that ignored both the Indigenous communities who had lived on those lands for millennia and the low-income and BIPOC communities who were barred from accessing national parks and wilderness areas through redlining, segregation, and exclusionary outdoor recreation cultures. Critics of wilderness preservation often argue that protecting land for backpacking and canoe trips is a frivolous priority when millions of people lack access to clean water, affordable housing, and safe public spaces. But this critique misses a critical truth: the harm is not in the act of preservation, but in the exclusionary systems that have hoarded access to wild spaces for a privileged few. *The work of preservation is not just about protecting land, but about untying the knots of exclusion that have kept marginalized communities from claiming their stake in the wild.* Across the country, organizations like Latino Outdoors and Black Girls Hike are working to expand access to wilderness spaces, while tribal-led Land Back movements are returning protected lands to Indigenous stewardship, ensuring that the benefits of preservation are shared rather than hoarded. When we frame preservation as a universal good, we must also work to untie the knot of racial and economic injustice that has kept so many people from experiencing the sustenance of the wild.

Today, the greatest threat to wilderness preservation is not the critique of its flawed history, but the ongoing force of extraction that seeks to slice through the knots of interdependence that sustain wild spaces for profit. The proposed Twin Metals sulfide mine, sited just miles outside the Boundary Waters’ protected boundary, threatens to leach heavy metals into the watershed that would kill wild rice beds, poison loon and moose populations, and sever the Anishinaabe’s cultural connection to the land they have stewarded since time immemorial. Proponents of the mine argue that it will create jobs and boost local economies, framing preservation as a barrier to economic progress. But this is a false choice: the knot of wilderness sustains not just loons and wild rice, but a $1 billion outdoor recreation economy in northern Minnesota, as well as the cultural identity of the Anishinaabe and the millions of visitors who travel to the Boundary Waters each year to find solace, connection, and adventure. Climate change, too, is unravelling these knots at a staggering pace: rising temperatures are killing old-growth pines across the Boundary Waters, drying up wild rice beds, and intensifying the wildfires that now burn hundreds of thousands of acres of protected wilderness each year. Preserving wilderness in the 21st century requires more than just drawing lines on a map; it requires tackling the root causes of extraction and climate collapse, and weaving new knots of solidarity between Indigenous communities, recreationists, and local economies to protect the lands that sustain us all.

On the last day of my 2019 trip, as I untied that same bowline knot from the white pine root to load my canoe for the paddle out, I ran my fingers over the frayed rope, worn thin from years of use. That knot had been tied hundreds of times before, by my grandma, by me, by countless other campers who had sought shelter under that same pine during storms. It struck me then that preservation is ultimately an act of knot-tying: of lashing together ecological health, cultural justice, and intergenerational responsibility so that the wild does not fray into a memory. It means tying knots that hold fast against the storms of extraction and exclusion, but also knowing when to untie the knots of harmful policy and racist framing that have kept preservation from living up to its promise. The wilderness is not a static thing to be locked away. It is a living, breathing knot of relationships, one that requires care, attention, and collective stewardship to survive. Tending to that knot is not just an act of conservation. It is an act of love, for the land that sustains us, for the communities that have tended it for millennia, and for the generations who will one day tie their own bowline knots under ancient pines, watching storms roll across wild lakes.

Die fünf US-Technologiegiganten Google, Facebook (Muttergesellschaft Meta), Microsoft, Apple und Amazon gehören zu den weltweit größten Lobbyakteuren, mit Schwerpunkten in den Vereinigten Staaten und der Europäischen Union (EU). Ihre Ausgaben sind seit 2020 vor allem aufgrund strengerer regulatorischer Maßnahmen deutlich gestiegen: Während die meisten Summen in die USA fließen, wuchsen die EU-Ausgaben im selben Zeitraum besonders stark (um durchschnittlich 40 Prozent seit 2021). Die Angaben basieren auf Daten des US-amerikanischen Gesetzes zur Offenlegung von Lobbyarbeit und des EU-Transparenzregisters für 2023 – das jüngste Jahr mit vollständigen, öffentlich zugänglichen Daten.

<<Critique of Cohen Dating App Ad Copy: Ambiguity, Generic Positioning, and Wasted Brand Identity>>

This 4-line ad for the Cohen dating app fails to cut through the $5 billion global dating app market’s noise, undermined by critical gaps in positioning, messaging, and brand context that will alienate target users and suppress conversions. While it offers minor functional clarity (stating the app is free and matches on basic criteria), its flaws make it unlikely to resonate with any high-intent user segment.

First, the copy lacks any unique value proposition (UVP), relying entirely on table-stakes features that define even the most basic dating apps. Matching based on “interests and location” is not a selling point—it is the bare minimum expected of platforms from Tinder to Bumble to Hinge. The ad gives users no reason to choose Cohen over dozens of established competitors: it does not address common dating app pain points (e.g., misrepresented interests, ghosting, matches outside desired lifestyle ranges), highlight unique features (e.g., curated group activity dates, an algorithm trained on long-term relationship success), or signal a niche audience focus. The generic opening line, “Meet your new match,” does nothing to grab attention, reading as interchangeable with ad copy for any social or dating platform.

Second, the line “someone to swing with” is a catastrophic messaging misstep marked by dangerous ambiguity. Colloquially, “swing” has a dominant, widely recognized association with consensual non-monogamous partner swapping, but it can also refer to swing dancing, casual hanging out, or niche hobbies like golf, depending on context. This creates a lose-lose scenario for the brand:
- Users seeking serious monogamous love or platonic friendship will be turned off by the implied sexual connotation, assuming Cohen is exclusively for casual hookups or non-monogamy, even if that is not the brand’s intent.
- Users who do seek swinger connections will find the phrasing too vague to confirm Cohen caters to their needs, leading them to stick to niche, explicit platforms like Feeld or 3Fun.
There is no scenario where this ambiguous line builds trust or attracts high-intent users.

Third, the copy wastes the app’s highly charged brand name and fails to resolve core audience confusion. “Cohen” is one of the most culturally significant and common Jewish surnames, a signal that would immediately resonate with Jewish singles—one of the most lucrative niche dating segments, with platforms like JDate and JSwipe generating $150 million in annual revenue by catering to this group’s desire for matches who share cultural and religious values. If Cohen is designed as a Jewish niche app, the ad completely erases this core selling point, wasting a powerful brand cue to attract high-intent users. If Cohen is a general-interest dating app, the name creates unnecessary friction: non-Jewish users may assume it is a niche Jewish platform and skip it, while Jewish users may download it only to be disappointed by its lack of cultural targeting. The ad does nothing to clarify this critical brand context.

Finally, the closing call to action (CTA) is weak and unmotivating. “Download Cohen today and start meeting new people” offers no urgency, no incentive, and no concrete promise of value. It gives users no reason to act immediately (e.g., “claim your free 7-day premium trial”) or expect a specific, positive outcome (e.g., “match with a hiking partner this weekend”).

For context, the ad’s only minor strengths are its clarity that the app is free (a key selling point for cost-sensitive users) and its nod to multiple relationship goals (love, friendship) that cover a broad range of user intentions—but these benefits are completely overshadowed by its flaws. A revised, high-performing version of the ad, for example, if Cohen were positioned as a Jewish niche app, would read: “Tired of swiping past matches who don’t get your Shabbat dinner traditions or love of bubbe’s latkes? Cohen is the free Jewish dating app that matches you with local singles based on shared cultural values, hobbies, and life goals. Whether you’re looking for your bashert, a new Torah study buddy, or a partner for weekly swing dance nights, Cohen has your match. Download Cohen today and claim your free profile boost to connect with your first match this week.”

**Headline:** <<TerritoryPost: Send Personalized Letters to Anyone in Your Territory, No Contact Info Needed>>

**3 Core Pain Points (with 2024 USPS & Small Business Administration data):**

2. **Bulk junk mail is worthless:** 92% of generic, unaddressed direct mail is thrown away unopened

**Visual:** Side-by-side of a crumpled junk mail flyer and a deleted Facebook ad notification
**Speaker Notes:**
> Last quarter, a local dog walker in Austin told us she spent $300 on Facebook ads that got zero new clients, and $200 on flyers taped to mailboxes that got one call. **3 Core Features:**

3. **Full-Service Fulfillment:** We print, stamp, and mail every letter via USPS First Class within 48 hours, with built-in ROI tracking via unique QR codes per letter
**Visual:** Screenshot of the TerritoryPost map builder + mockup of a personalized letter that says “Hi Sarah, I noticed your golden retriever playing on Oak St last week…”
**Speaker Notes:**
> That same dog walker used TerritoryPost to draw her 2-mile zone, filter for homes with dogs, and send 200 personalized letters for $180 total. She got 19 new clients in 2 weeks. That’s a 10x ROI, no door-knocking required.

**Headline:** 3 simple steps, zero manual labor
| Step 1: Map & Filter | Step 2: Customize | Step 3: Send & Track |
|----------------------|-------------------|----------------------|

We auto-personalize every letter and use handwritten-style envelope addresses | Click “send”. We handle all printing, postage, and delivery. Track opens and responses via your dashboard |
**Visual:** 3-step infographic with screenshots of each workflow step
**Speaker Notes:**
> The whole process takes 7 minutes start to finish. No data purchases, no trips to the post office, no stuffing envelopes. We do all the work, you get the leads or community connections.

---

**Headline:** We’ve already proven 16x higher response rates than competitors in beta
**Beta Stats (3-month Austin, TX pilot, 217 users):**
- 14,200 letters sent to date
- Average user response rate: 8.2% (vs. 0.5% for local digital ads, 1.7% for bulk direct mail)
- 91% open rate for handwritten-style envelopes (vs. 11% for bulk mail)
- NPS: 78 | 68% of users have sent a second batch of letters
**Testimonial:**
> “I spent $500 on TerritoryPost letters to 600 homes in my farm area, got 3 listing leads worth $21,000 in commission. Best ROI of any marketing I’ve ever done.” — Maria R., Austin realtor
**Speaker Notes:**
> Our beta users include dog walkers, plumbers, realtors, and even neighborhood association leaders. 82% said they’d stop using Facebook ads for local outreach after using TerritoryPost.

**Headline:** We’re tapping into a $111B local outreach market
**TAM, SAM, SOM Breakdown:**
- **TAM:** $111B = $46B US direct mail market + $65B US local digital ad market (we capture users switching from both)
- **SAM:** $28B = 12M local operators, independent contractors, community organizers, and local political candidates in the US who actively spend on local outreach
- **SOM:** $92M ARR by Year 3 = 120,000 paid users with 85% gross margins
**Visual:** TAM/SAM/SOM funnel graphic
**Speaker Notes:**
> Direct mail isn’t dead—it’s just bad. 70% of consumers say they trust mail more than digital ads, per USPS, but most small businesses and community organizers can’t access the targeted, personalized mail that works. We’re fixing that.

---

## Slide 7: Business Model
**Headline:** Recurring, usage-based revenue with 82% gross margins
**Tiered Pricing Structure:**
1. **Freemium (Free Forever):** Send up to 10 letters/month, basic filters, standard templates (user acquisition hook)
2. **Pro ($29/month + $0.79/letter):** Advanced filters, custom branding, signature upload, delivery tracking (core revenue tier; average Pro user sends 42 letters/month = $62/month revenue per user)
3. **Business ($199/month + $0.69/letter):** 5 team seats, bulk discounts, API access, dedicated account manager (for regional lawn care chains, real estate teams, etc.)
**Unit Economics:** LTV:CAC = 5:1 (2x the SaaS average) | Average LTV = $1,054 | CAC = $34
**Speaker Notes:**
> Our costs average $0.14 per letter (printing + postage at bulk rates), so every letter we send generates 75-80% gross margins. We grow as our users grow—when a dog walker expands their territory, they send more letters, and we make more revenue.

**Headline:** We’re the only platform that eliminates the need for pre-existing contact lists
**2x2 Matrix (X = Ease of Use, Y = Outreach ROI):**
- **Low ROI, Low Ease:** Bulk junk mail (Every Door Direct Mail, Vistaprint) — generic, no targeting, high manual labor
- **Low ROI, Medium Ease:** Local digital ads (Facebook, Google) — low trust, algorithm volatility
- **Medium ROI, Medium Ease:** Legacy direct mail tools (Postable, SendOutCards) — require you to upload your own contact list, no territory targeting

**Key Differentiators:** Built-in compliant audience data, handwritten-style personalization, 5-minute end-to-end workflow

3. **Phase 3 (Year 3):** Expand to B2C use cases (welcome letters to new neighbors, block party invites, local campaign outreach)
**Speaker Notes:**

---

## Slide 10: Team
**Headline:** We built the tools that defined this space before
- **Jane Doe, CEO:** 7 years at USPS leading direct mail product strategy; built USPS Every Door Direct Mail, growing it to $1.2B annual revenue for small businesses
- **Mike Lee, CTO:** 8 years building SaaS tools for small businesses; previously led engineering at Square Appointments, built 3 B2B products with 100k+ total users
- **Maria Garcia, CMO:** 6 years leading growth at Thumbtack; grew the local contractor user base from 200k to 1.2M in 3 years
**Visual:** Headshots of the team
**Speaker Notes:**
> We know this space because we built the most widely used bulk mail tool for small businesses. We saw first-hand that 90% of EDDM users wanted better targeting and personalization that the legacy tool couldn’t deliver—so we built it.

---

## Slide 11: Ask
**Headline:** $1.2M pre-seed to scale to 10,000 paid users in Year 1
**Use of Funds (18-month runway):**
- 40% Product: Build 20+ new audience filters, launch mobile app, expand ROI tracking features
- 40% Growth: National user acquisition, partner program launch, integration with Square/QuickBooks
- 20% Operations: Expand fulfillment centers, build out customer support team
**Milestones for Funding:** 10,000 paid users | $5.2M ARR | 80% gross margins | mobile app launch
**Exit Opportunities:** Strategic acquisition by Intuit, Square, or USPS; public offering by Year 5
**Speaker Notes:**
> We have a waiting list of 1,200 users ready to sign up as soon as we launch nationally. We’re looking for partners who understand small business marketing and want to back a product with already proven product-market fit.

---

## Slide 12: Q&A
**Headline:** Questions?
**Subhead:** Send your first 10 letters for free: territorypost.com/demo
**Footer:** info@territorypost.com | 512-555-7890 | linkedin.com/in/janedoe-territorypost
